elements.name: Chlorine

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.description: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that is poisonous to breathe — but that same germ-killing power, used carefully, makes drinking water safe and keeps swimming pools clean. Joined to sodium it becomes the salt on your fries.
funFacts: Adding chlorine to drinking water is one of the greatest public-health inventions ever.
That 'swimming pool smell' is not chlorine — it is chlorine reacting with sweat and skin.
Chlorine gas is heavier than air, so it sinks and pools on the ground.
Your stomach uses chlorine as hydrochloric acid to digest food.
PVC pipes and raincoats are plastics made with chlorine.

compounds.name: Sodium chloride
compounds.about: Table salt, and the salt that makes the sea salty.

compounds.name: Hydrochloric acid
compounds.about: Made by your stomach to break down food.

compounds.name: Sodium hypochlorite
compounds.about: Household bleach and pool disinfectant.

compounds.name: PVC
compounds.about: The plastic in pipes, flooring and raincoats.

compounds.name: Potassium chloride
compounds.about: A fertilizer, and a low-sodium salt substitute.

compounds.name: Calcium chloride
compounds.about: Melts ice on roads and warms up when it dissolves.

compounds.name: Chloroform
compounds.about: An old-fashioned anesthetic, now used as a lab solvent.

compounds.name: Ammonium chloride
compounds.about: Used in batteries and in salty Nordic licorice candy.

compounds.name: Silver chloride
compounds.about: Darkens in sunlight — the basis of old photography.

compounds.name: Magnesium chloride
compounds.about: Extracted from seawater; used for de-icing and making tofu.

elements.name: Argon

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.description: Argon's name literally means 'the lazy one', because it will not react with anything. That laziness is its superpower: fill a space with argon and nothing inside can burn, rust or spoil. It is the third most common gas in the air, about 1% of every breath.
funFacts: Almost 1% of the air you breathe is argon, yet nobody noticed it until 1894.
Welders blow argon over hot metal so it cannot react with oxygen.
Double-glazed windows are filled with argon to keep houses warm.
Museums store fragile old documents under argon to stop them decaying.
Old light bulbs used argon so the glowing filament would not burn away.
elements.compoundsNote: Argon is a noble gas and forms no compounds under normal conditions. Only one has ever been made: argon fluorohydride (HArF), created in 2000 at −265 °C, which falls apart the moment it warms up.

compoundsExamples.name: Argon fluorohydride
compoundsExamples.about: The only known argon compound; survives only at extreme cold.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.nameMeaning: From potash; symbol K from Latin kalium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Potassium is even more excitable than sodium — a small piece dropped in water skitters about and bursts into a lilac flame. Locked safely into compounds it is one of the three nutrients every plant needs, and your heart uses it for every single beat.
funFacts: Potassium reacts with water so fast that it sets the hydrogen it releases on fire.
Bananas are famous for potassium — you would need to eat many thousands for it to be risky.
Every heartbeat depends on potassium moving in and out of your cells.
A tiny fraction of natural potassium is radioactive, so bananas are very slightly radioactive.
Potassium burns with a beautiful lilac-purple flame.

compounds.name: Potassium chloride
compounds.about: The world's main potassium fertilizer, mined as potash.

compounds.name: Potassium nitrate
compounds.about: Saltpetre — a fertilizer and part of gunpowder.

compounds.name: Potassium hydroxide
compounds.about: Used to make soft soaps and in alkaline batteries.

compounds.name: Potassium carbonate
compounds.about: Potash — originally made from wood ash in iron pots.

compounds.name: Potassium permanganate
compounds.about: Deep purple crystals used as a disinfectant.

compounds.name: Orthoclase feldspar
compounds.about: A very common pink mineral in granite.

compounds.name: Potassium iodide
compounds.about: Added to table salt to prevent thyroid illness.

compounds.name: Potassium sulfate
compounds.about: A fertilizer for crops that dislike chloride.

compounds.name: Cream of tartar
compounds.about: A baking powder ingredient that comes from wine barrels.

compounds.name: Potassium dichromate
compounds.about: Bright orange crystals used as a strong laboratory oxidizer.

elements.name: Calcium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Calcium is the element that builds skeletons. Your bones and teeth, seashells, coral reefs, chalk cliffs and eggshells are all calcium compounds. It is the fifth most common element in the Earth's crust and the most common metal in your body.
funFacts: About 99% of the calcium in your body is stored in your bones and teeth.
The White Cliffs of Dover are made of billions of tiny calcium shells from ancient sea creatures.
Cement, concrete and plaster all start from calcium compounds.
Pure calcium metal is silvery and soft, and most people never see it.
Your muscles cannot contract at all without calcium — including your heart.

compounds.name: Calcium carbonate
compounds.about: Limestone, chalk, marble, seashells and eggshells.

compounds.name: Calcium phosphate
compounds.about: The mineral that makes bones and teeth strong.

compounds.name: Gypsum
compounds.about: Drywall, plaster casts and blackboard chalk.

compounds.name: Calcium oxide
compounds.about: Quicklime — gets scorching hot when water is added.

compounds.name: Calcium hydroxide
compounds.about: Slaked lime, used in mortar and to treat sour soil.

compounds.name: Calcium chloride
compounds.about: Melts road ice even in very cold weather.

compounds.name: Fluorite
compounds.about: A colorful mineral that glows under ultraviolet light.

compounds.name: Calcium carbide
compounds.about: Add water and it makes a gas that burns in miners' lamps.

compounds.name: Calcium nitrate
compounds.about: A fertilizer that gives plants both calcium and nitrogen.

compounds.name: Dolomite
compounds.about: The rock that forms the Dolomite mountains in Italy.

elements.name: Scandium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Scandium is a light silvery metal that Dmitri Mendeleev predicted before anyone found it — he left a gap in his periodic table and described what should fill it. Ten years later scandium turned up in Scandinavian rock, almost exactly as he had said.
funFacts: Mendeleev predicted scandium's existence and properties a decade before it was discovered.
Adding a pinch of scandium to aluminum makes bike frames and jet parts much stronger.
Scandium lamps make a light so like sunlight that stadiums use them for TV cameras.
It is not actually rare in the crust, but it is spread so thinly that it is hard to gather.
Most scandium comes as a by-product of mining other metals.

compounds.name: Scandium oxide
compounds.about: The most common scandium chemical, used in stadium lamps.

compounds.name: Scandium fluoride
compounds.about: Strangely, it shrinks when heated instead of expanding.

compounds.name: Scandium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make pure scandium metal.

compounds.name: Scandium hydroxide
compounds.about: A step in purifying scandium from its ore.

compounds.name: Scandium phosphate
compounds.about: Found in trace amounts in phosphate rocks.

compounds.name: Scandium sulfate
compounds.about: Once tested as a seed treatment for crops.

compounds.name: Scandium iodide
compounds.about: The ingredient that gives metal-halide lamps daylight color.

compounds.name: Scandium boride
compounds.about: A very hard ceramic material.

compounds.name: Scandium nitride
compounds.about: A semiconductor studied for electronics.

compounds.name: Thortveitite
compounds.about: The rare Norwegian mineral with the most scandium in it.

elements.name: Titanium
elements.nameMeaning: After the Titans of Greek myth

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Titanium is as strong as steel but nearly half the weight, and it never rusts — even in seawater. It is also friendly to the human body, so surgeons use it for hip replacements and dental implants. It is named after the Titans, the giants of Greek mythology.
funFacts: Titanium is so body-friendly that bone grows straight onto a titanium implant.
Spacecraft, submarines and the fastest jets all use titanium parts.
Titanium dioxide is the whitest white known — it is in paint, sunscreen and toothpaste.
It is the ninth most common element in the crust, but very expensive to purify.
Titanium sparks and burns fiercely as a powder, though solid lumps are safe.

compounds.name: Titanium dioxide
compounds.about: The brilliant white pigment in paint, sunscreen and icing.

compounds.name: Ilmenite
compounds.about: The main ore that titanium is mined from.

compounds.name: Titanium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A liquid that makes thick white smoke in air — used for skywriting.

compounds.name: Titanium nitride
compounds.about: The gold-colored coating on drill bits that keeps them sharp.

compounds.name: Titanium carbide
compounds.about: Extremely hard; used on cutting tools.

compounds.name: Perovskite
compounds.about: Gives its name to a crystal shape used in new solar panels.

compounds.name: Barium titanate
compounds.about: Makes electricity when squeezed; used in microphones.

compounds.name: Titanium(III) oxide
compounds.about: A purple oxide studied for its unusual electrical behavior.

compounds.name: Titanium hydride
compounds.about: A gray powder used to make metal foams.

compounds.name: Titanium diboride
compounds.about: A ceramic tough enough for armor plating.

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.nameMeaning: After Vanadis, a Norse goddess of beauty

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Vanadium is the rainbow element: its compounds come in purple, green, blue and yellow, depending on how many electrons it has given away. Add a little vanadium to steel and it becomes tough enough for wrenches, springs and armor.
funFacts: Vanadium solutions change color through purple, green, blue and yellow like a science rainbow.
It is named after a Norse goddess of beauty because its compounds are so colorful.
Henry Ford used vanadium steel to make the Model T lighter and stronger.
Some sea squirts collect vanadium in their blood and nobody is quite sure why.
Giant vanadium flow batteries store electricity for whole towns.

compounds.name: Vanadium pentoxide
compounds.about: An orange powder that helps make sulfuric acid.

compounds.name: Vanadium dioxide
compounds.about: Switches from insulator to metal when warmed — used in smart windows.

compounds.name: Vanadium trichloride
compounds.about: Purple crystals used in chemistry labs.

compounds.name: Vanadyl sulfate
compounds.about: Bright blue; used in vanadium flow batteries.

compounds.name: Vanadium nitride
compounds.about: A hard coating that strengthens steel.

compounds.name: Vanadium carbide
compounds.about: Keeps steel grains tiny, making tools stronger.

compounds.name: Vanadinite
compounds.about: A beautiful red crystal mineral and a vanadium ore.

compounds.name: Vanadium gallium
compounds.about: A superconductor used in very strong magnets.

compounds.name: Ammonium metavanadate
compounds.about: A step in refining vanadium from ore.

compounds.name: Carnotite
compounds.about: A yellow mineral holding both vanadium and uranium.

elements.name: Chromium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Chromium is the mirror-shiny metal that makes chrome bumpers and faucets sparkle, and it is what makes stainless steel stainless. Its name means 'color' because chromium compounds are wildly colorful — a chromium atom is why a ruby is red and an emerald is green.
funFacts: The same element makes rubies red and emeralds green; it depends on the crystal around it.
Stainless steel resists rust because chromium forms an invisible protective skin.
Chrome plating is a paper-thin layer of chromium over another metal.
Chromium is the hardest metal in its pure form on some scratch tests.
The yellow of old school buses came from a chromium pigment.

compounds.name: Chromite
compounds.about: The only ore chromium is mined from.

compounds.name: Chromium(III) oxide
compounds.about: A tough green pigment used in paints and polish.

compounds.name: Chromium trioxide
compounds.about: Dark red crystals used for chrome plating.

compounds.name: Potassium dichromate
compounds.about: Bright orange; a powerful laboratory oxidizer.

compounds.name: Lead chromate
compounds.about: 'Chrome yellow' — the classic bright yellow paint pigment.

compounds.name: Chromium(III) chloride
compounds.about: Purple flakes used to make other chromium chemicals.

compounds.name: Chromium sulfate
compounds.about: Used to tan leather so it stays soft and lasts.

compounds.name: Chromium dioxide
compounds.about: Magnetic — it recorded sound on high-quality cassette tapes.

compounds.name: Chromium nitrate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used to prepare catalysts.

compounds.name: Chromium nitride
compounds.about: A hard coating that stops tools wearing out.

elements.name: Manganese
elements.nameMeaning: From Magnesia, a district in Greece

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Manganese is a hard, brittle gray metal that makes steel far tougher — railroad tracks and excavator teeth are made of manganese steel. Plants and animals need it too, and it plays a starring role in photosynthesis, helping split water to release oxygen.
funFacts: Without manganese, plants could not release the oxygen you breathe.
Manganese steel is so tough it gets harder the more you hammer it.
Cave painters 30,000 years ago used black manganese minerals for their pictures.
The deep ocean floor is scattered with potato-sized lumps called manganese nodules.
Purple potassium permanganate turns water bright pink at incredible dilutions.

compounds.name: Manganese dioxide
compounds.about: The black powder inside ordinary batteries.

compounds.name: Potassium permanganate
compounds.about: Deep purple crystals used to disinfect water.

compounds.name: Manganese sulfate
compounds.about: A fertilizer and animal feed supplement.

compounds.name: Rhodochrosite
compounds.about: A pretty pink banded gemstone mineral.

compounds.name: Hausmannite
compounds.about: A manganese ore mineral.

compounds.name: Manganese chloride
compounds.about: Pale pink crystals used in medicine and batteries.

compounds.name: Manganese(II) oxide
compounds.about: Green powder added to fertilizer and glass.

compounds.name: Manganese sulfide
compounds.about: Forms in steel and helps it machine smoothly.

compounds.name: Lithium manganese oxide
compounds.about: A safe battery material used in power tools.

compounds.name: Manganese ferrite
compounds.about: A magnetic ceramic used in electronics.

elements.name: Iron
elements.nameMeaning: From Old English iren; symbol Fe from Latin ferrum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Iron is the metal that built the modern world: bridges, ships, cars, skyscrapers and railroads are all mostly iron turned into steel. It is also inside you — iron in your blood grabs oxygen from your lungs and carries it around your body, and it is what makes blood red.
funFacts: Your blood is red because of iron; some sea creatures use copper instead and have blue blood.
The Earth's core is a giant ball of iron, and it makes our planet's magnetic field.
Iron is the heaviest element that stars can make by normal fusion.
The first iron humans used came from meteorites and was called 'metal from the sky'.
An average adult carries about 4 grams of iron — roughly one small nail's worth.

compounds.name: Hematite
compounds.about: The main iron ore, and the rust that makes Mars red.

compounds.name: Magnetite
compounds.about: Naturally magnetic — the original lodestone compasses.

compounds.name: Pyrite
compounds.about: 'Fool's gold', shiny golden cubes of iron and sulfur.

compounds.name: Siderite
compounds.about: An iron carbonate mineral and minor ore.

compounds.name: Iron(II) sulfate
compounds.about: An iron supplement for people and for plants.

compounds.name: Hemoglobin
compounds.about: The iron protein that carries oxygen in your blood.

compounds.name: Iron(III) chloride
compounds.about: Used to clean water and to etch circuit boards.

compounds.name: Cementite
compounds.about: The hard iron-carbon crystal that makes steel strong.

compounds.name: Goethite
compounds.about: The brown-yellow mineral in ochre paints.

compounds.name: Prussian blue precursor
compounds.about: Leads to Prussian blue, the first modern synthetic pigment.

elements.name: Cobalt

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Cobalt is named after goblins — German miners blamed mischievous kobolds when the ore they dug made them sick and gave no useful metal. Today cobalt gives us the deepest blue in glass and pottery, and it is a vital ingredient in rechargeable batteries.
funFacts: Cobalt blue glass and pottery glazes have been used for over 4,000 years.
Vitamin B12, which your nerves need, has a cobalt atom at its center.
Cobalt is magnetic and keeps its magnetism even when very hot.
Radioactive cobalt-60 is used to treat cancer and sterilize medical tools.
Some cobalt salts change color with humidity, so they work as weather predictors.

compounds.name: Cobalt blue
compounds.about: The intense blue pigment in glass, paint and pottery.

compounds.name: Lithium cobalt oxide
compounds.about: The cathode in most phone and laptop batteries.

compounds.name: Cobalt chloride
compounds.about: Pink when damp, blue when dry — an old humidity indicator.

compounds.name: Vitamin B12
compounds.about: The only vitamin that contains a metal atom.

compounds.name: Cobalt(II) oxide
compounds.about: Used to color glass and ceramics.

compounds.name: Cobalt sulfate
compounds.about: Used in electroplating and animal feed.

compounds.name: Cobaltite
compounds.about: A silvery ore mineral of cobalt.

compounds.name: Cobalt(II,III) oxide
compounds.about: A black powder used as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Samarium cobalt
compounds.about: A super-strong magnet that works at high temperatures.

compounds.name: Cobalt fluoride
compounds.about: Pink crystals used to make fluorine compounds.

elements.name: Nickel

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Nickel is a tough, silvery metal that hardly corrodes, so it is mixed into stainless steel and plated onto shiny things. Together with iron it fills the Earth's core, and it makes up much of the metal in iron meteorites that fall from space.
funFacts: The Earth's core is mostly iron and nickel, over 5,000 °C and under huge pressure.
Nickel got its name from miners who thought a devil had spoiled their copper ore.
Many coins are nickel — the US five-cent piece is even nicknamed 'a nickel'.
Nickel-metal-hydride batteries powered the first hybrid cars.
Some people are allergic to nickel and get a rash from cheap jewelry.

compounds.name: Nickel oxide
compounds.about: Green powder used in ceramics and batteries.

compounds.name: Millerite
compounds.about: A golden needle-like nickel ore mineral.

compounds.name: Nickel sulfate
compounds.about: Blue-green crystals used for nickel plating.

compounds.name: Nickel chloride
compounds.about: Yellow-green salt used in electroplating baths.

compounds.name: Nickel hydroxide
compounds.about: The active material in rechargeable NiMH batteries.

compounds.name: Pentlandite
compounds.about: The world's most important nickel ore.

compounds.name: Nickel carbonyl
compounds.about: A liquid used to make ultra-pure nickel — and very poisonous.

compounds.name: Nitinol
compounds.about: A 'memory metal' that springs back to its original shape when warmed.

compounds.name: Nickeline
compounds.about: The copper-colored ore that fooled early miners.

compounds.name: Nickel ferrite
compounds.about: A magnetic ceramic used in electronic parts.

elements.name: Copper
elements.nameMeaning: From Cyprus, the island; Latin cuprum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Copper was the first metal humans ever worked with, over 10,000 years ago, because lumps of it can be found pure in the ground. It carries electricity better than almost anything else affordable, so the wires in your walls and the cables in your charger are copper.
funFacts: The Bronze Age began when people mixed copper with tin to make bronze.
The Statue of Liberty is copper — it turned green from a hundred years of weather.
Copper kills germs on contact, so hospitals use copper door handles.
Nearly every electrical wire in your home is copper.
Copper is one of very few metals with a color of its own, rather than plain silver-gray.

compounds.name: Copper sulfate
compounds.about: Vivid blue crystals; a classic school science chemical.

compounds.name: Chalcopyrite
compounds.about: The world's main copper ore, a brassy yellow mineral.

compounds.name: Copper(I) oxide
compounds.about: A red powder used in anti-fouling paint for ships.

compounds.name: Copper(II) oxide
compounds.about: Black powder used as a pigment and catalyst.

compounds.name: Malachite
compounds.about: A gorgeous banded green gemstone and old copper ore.

compounds.name: Azurite
compounds.about: A deep blue mineral once ground up for paint.

compounds.name: Copper(II) chloride
compounds.about: Turns flames blue-green; used in fireworks.

compounds.name: Chalcocite
compounds.about: A dark gray ore rich in copper.

compounds.name: Copper hydroxide
compounds.about: A blue powder used as a garden fungicide.

compounds.name: Verdigris
compounds.about: The green coating on old copper roofs and statues.

elements.name: Zinc

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Zinc's great trick is sacrificing itself: coat iron in zinc and the zinc corrodes first, protecting the iron underneath. That is galvanizing, and it keeps buckets, nails and lamp posts from rusting away. Your body needs zinc too, for healing cuts and fighting colds.
funFacts: Galvanized metal is steel wearing a zinc coat that rusts instead of the steel.
Zinc is in over 300 different enzymes in your body.
A modern penny is mostly zinc with only a thin copper skin.
Zinc oxide is the white paste lifeguards put on their noses to block the sun.
Brass, used in trumpets and door handles, is copper mixed with zinc.

compounds.name: Zinc oxide
compounds.about: White sunblock paste, and a soothing diaper rash cream.

compounds.name: Sphalerite
compounds.about: The main zinc ore; a form of it glows in the dark.

compounds.name: Zinc sulfate
compounds.about: A supplement for crops growing in poor soil.

compounds.name: Zinc chloride
compounds.about: Helps solder stick to metal, and preserves wood.

compounds.name: Smithsonite
compounds.about: A colorful mineral and secondary zinc ore.

compounds.name: Zinc stearate
compounds.about: A slippery powder used to stop things sticking.

compounds.name: Zinc phosphate
compounds.about: A rust-proofing primer under car paint.

compounds.name: Zinc selenide
compounds.about: A crystal that lets infrared laser light pass through.

compounds.name: Zinc hydroxide
compounds.about: Used in surgical dressings to absorb fluid.

compounds.name: Zinc pyrithione
compounds.about: The anti-dandruff ingredient in shampoo.

elements.name: Gallium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Gallium is the metal that melts in your hand — its melting point is just below body temperature, so a solid lump turns into a silvery puddle in your palm. It is the key ingredient in LEDs, the tiny lights in screens, flashlights and traffic signals.
funFacts: A gallium spoon melts away when you stir a hot drink — a classic magic trick.
Gallium melts at 30 °C but does not boil until 2,400 °C, the widest liquid range of any metal.
Blue LEDs, which made white LED lighting possible, are made from gallium nitride.
Mendeleev predicted gallium too, calling it 'eka-aluminum'.
Gallium sticks to glass, so it leaves a mirror-like smear.

compounds.name: Gallium nitride
compounds.about: Makes blue and white LEDs and fast phone chargers.

compounds.name: Gallium arsenide
compounds.about: Used in solar cells for satellites and in fast radio chips.

compounds.name: Gallium oxide
compounds.about: A clear material studied for high-power electronics.

compounds.name: Gallium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make other gallium chemicals.

compounds.name: Gallium phosphide
compounds.about: Makes green and yellow LED lights.

compounds.name: Indium gallium nitride
compounds.about: The exact layer that glows blue inside an LED.

compounds.name: Gallium antimonide
compounds.about: Detects infrared light in night-vision devices.

compounds.name: Gallium nitrate
compounds.about: A medicine used to treat high blood calcium.

compounds.name: Gallium sulfide
compounds.about: A layered crystal studied for electronics.

compounds.name: CIGS
compounds.about: A thin, bendy solar panel material.

elements.name: Germanium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Germanium was the material in the very first transistors, the tiny switches that started the computer age, before silicon took over. Today it works quietly inside fiber-optic cables and infrared night-vision cameras, letting light and heat travel where we need them.
funFacts: The first transistor, built in 1947, was made of germanium.
Germanium is see-through to infrared light, so thermal cameras use germanium lenses.
The glass fibers carrying the internet under the oceans contain germanium.
Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-silicon' 15 years before it was found.
Like water, germanium expands when it freezes.

compounds.name: Germanium dioxide
compounds.about: Added to optical fiber glass to guide light.

compounds.name: Germanium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A liquid used to make optical fibers.

compounds.name: Silicon germanium
compounds.about: Speeds up chips in phones and satellites.

compounds.name: Germane
compounds.about: A gas used to lay down germanium layers on chips.

compounds.name: Germanite
compounds.about: A rare mineral that actually contains germanium.

compounds.name: Germanium disulfide
compounds.about: Used in infrared glasses.

compounds.name: Germanium telluride
compounds.about: Switches states quickly; used in rewritable memory.

compounds.name: Germanium nitride
compounds.about: A thin insulating layer in electronics.

compounds.name: Germanium selenide
compounds.about: Studied for thin solar cells.

compounds.name: GST
compounds.about: The material that stores data on rewritable DVDs.

elements.name: Arsenic
elements.nameMeaning: From Greek arsenikon, a yellow mineral

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.description: Arsenic is famous as the poison of history — it has no taste or smell, so it was once called 'inheritance powder'. But arsenic is not all bad: it makes the fast chips in cell phones work, and a careful dose of it is a modern cure for one kind of leukemia.
funFacts: Arsenic is tasteless and odorless, which is why it was history's favorite poison.
Victorian wallpaper contained a green arsenic pigment that slowly made people ill.
A tiny controlled dose of arsenic trioxide now cures a type of leukemia.
Gallium arsenide chips help your phone talk to cell towers.
Some groundwater naturally contains dangerous arsenic, a serious problem in parts of Asia.

compounds.name: Arsenic trioxide
compounds.about: The classic poison, now also a leukemia medicine.

compounds.name: Gallium arsenide
compounds.about: Powers fast phone chips and space solar panels.

compounds.name: Arsenopyrite
compounds.about: The most common arsenic mineral, often found near gold.

compounds.name: Orpiment
compounds.about: A golden-yellow mineral used as paint by ancient artists.

compounds.name: Realgar
compounds.about: A ruby-red mineral that crumbles in sunlight.

compounds.name: Arsine
compounds.about: A very poisonous gas used in making semiconductors.

compounds.name: Arsenic acid
compounds.about: Once used in wood preservatives.

compounds.name: Paris green
compounds.about: A vivid green pigment and old insect killer.

compounds.name: Indium arsenide
compounds.about: Used in infrared detectors.

compounds.name: Aluminum arsenide
compounds.about: Layered with gallium arsenide inside lasers.

elements.name: Selenium

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.description: Selenium can see: it conducts electricity better in bright light than in the dark, which made it the heart of the first light meters and early photocopiers. Your body needs a tiny amount of selenium, but a little more than that is toxic — a very fine line.
funFacts: Selenium changes how well it conducts electricity depending on the light shining on it.
The first photocopiers used a selenium drum to catch the image.
Two brazil nuts give you all the selenium you need for a day.
Selenium turns glass a beautiful ruby red, and can also cancel out green tints.
It is named after the Moon, while its neighbor tellurium is named after the Earth.

compounds.name: Selenium dioxide
compounds.about: Used to give glass a red color.

compounds.name: Selenic acid
compounds.about: One of the few acids that can dissolve gold.

compounds.name: Sodium selenite
compounds.about: Added to animal feed and vitamin tablets.

compounds.name: Cadmium selenide
compounds.about: Makes quantum dots that glow pure colors in QLED TVs.

compounds.name: Hydrogen selenide
compounds.about: Smells even worse than rotten eggs and is very toxic.

compounds.name: Zinc selenide
compounds.about: A window material for infrared lasers.

compounds.name: Selenium disulfide
compounds.about: The active ingredient in anti-dandruff shampoo.

compounds.name: Copper indium selenide
compounds.about: Used in thin-film solar panels.

compounds.name: Lead selenide
compounds.about: Detects infrared light in heat sensors.

compounds.name: Selenium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A colorless gas used in electronics manufacturing.

elements.name: Bromine

zhRadical.note: The 氵(water) radical — bromine is a liquid.

elements.description: Bromine is one of only two elements that is a liquid at room temperature, and it is a startling red-brown that gives off choking orange fumes. Its name means 'stench'. Long ago, a related bromine compound from sea snails made the royal purple dye that only emperors could wear.
funFacts: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
Ancient Tyrian purple dye came from sea snails and contained bromine.
Bromine compounds were once added to sofas and TVs to stop them catching fire.
The Dead Sea is one of the world's richest sources of bromine.
It evaporates easily, filling a jar with thick orange-brown vapor.

compounds.name: Sodium bromide
compounds.about: Used to disinfect hot tubs, and once used as a medicine.

compounds.name: Potassium bromide
compounds.about: Used in old photography and as an animal medicine.

compounds.name: Silver bromide
compounds.about: The light-sensitive crystal in old photographic film.

compounds.name: Hydrobromic acid
compounds.about: A strong acid used to make other bromine chemicals.

compounds.name: Methyl bromide
compounds.about: A pesticide now restricted for harming the ozone layer.

compounds.name: Brominated flame retardants
compounds.about: Once added to electronics to slow burning.

compounds.name: Calcium bromide
compounds.about: A dense liquid used in oil drilling.

compounds.name: Bromothymol blue
compounds.about: A dye that turns yellow in acid and blue in alkali.

compounds.name: Magnesium bromide
compounds.about: Extracted from seawater and brine wells.

compounds.name: Tyrian purple
compounds.about: The ancient royal dye made from sea snails.

elements.name: Krypton

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.description: Krypton is a hidden gas — its name means exactly that, because it was so hard to find in the air. It is nearly as unreactive as its noble gas cousins, but chemists can force it to bond with fluorine. It has nothing at all to do with Superman's home planet.
funFacts: Krypton has no link to Superman — the planet was simply named after the gas.
For 23 years, the meter was officially defined by orange light from krypton atoms.
Krypton makes bright white light in high-speed photography flashes.
It fills some energy-saving double-glazed windows.
Krypton is only about one part per million of the air.

compounds.name: Krypton difluoride
compounds.about: The only well-studied krypton compound; it needs deep cold to survive.

elements.compoundsNote: Krypton is a noble gas, so it barely reacts. Krypton difluoride is essentially its only real compound; a handful of other fragile krypton molecules have been made in cold laboratory experiments.

elements.name: Rubidium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Rubidium is a soft silvery metal that reacts with water so violently it explodes, and it can catch fire just sitting in air. It was discovered by looking at the colors in a flame — it made two deep red lines nobody had seen before. Rubidium atoms keep time in some of the world's best clocks.
funFacts: Rubidium was discovered by its color in a flame, one of the first elements found that way.
It melts at just 39 °C — barely above a hot summer day.
Rubidium atomic clocks are accurate to a second in thousands of years.
Scientists chilled rubidium to make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a brand new state of matter.
It reacts so fast with water that it can shatter the container.

compounds.name: Rubidium chloride
compounds.about: Used in biology to help cells take up DNA.

compounds.name: Rubidium carbonate
compounds.about: Added to special glass for fiber optics.

compounds.name: Rubidium hydroxide
compounds.about: A very strong alkali used in some batteries.

compounds.name: Rubidium nitrate
compounds.about: Burns purple in fireworks and flares.

compounds.name: Rubidium sulfate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used in laboratories.

compounds.name: Rubidium iodide
compounds.about: Used in specialized optical equipment.

compounds.name: Rubidium fluoride
compounds.about: A salt used in chemistry research.

compounds.name: Rubidium superoxide
compounds.about: An orange solid that can release oxygen.

compounds.name: Rubidium silver iodide
compounds.about: Conducts electricity through moving ions at room temperature.

compounds.name: Rubidium hydride
compounds.about: A reactive solid used in chemical research.

elements.name: Strontium
elements.nameMeaning: From Strontian, a village in Scotland

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Strontium is the element that paints fireworks red — no other element gives quite that brilliant crimson. It is named after a tiny Scottish village where its ore was first found. Strontium behaves so much like calcium that your bones will absorb it by mistake.
funFacts: Every red firework you have ever seen was colored by strontium.
It is named after Strontian, a small village in the Scottish Highlands.
Glow-in-the-dark stars and watch hands use a strontium compound.
Because it acts like calcium, radioactive strontium from nuclear accidents ends up in bones.
Toothpaste for sensitive teeth often contains strontium.

compounds.name: Strontianite
compounds.about: The mineral used to make red firework stars.

compounds.name: Celestine
compounds.about: A sky-blue mineral and the main strontium ore.

compounds.name: Strontium nitrate
compounds.about: The classic red flare and firework chemical.

compounds.name: Strontium oxide
compounds.about: Was used in old television screen glass.

compounds.name: Strontium chloride
compounds.about: The ingredient in sensitive-teeth toothpaste.

compounds.name: Strontium titanate
compounds.about: Sparkles more than diamond; used as a fake gemstone.

compounds.name: Strontium aluminate
compounds.about: The best glow-in-the-dark material, glowing for hours.

compounds.name: Strontium ferrite
compounds.about: The cheap black magnets on your fridge.

compounds.name: Strontium hydroxide
compounds.about: Used to extract sugar from beet.

compounds.name: Strontium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in special optical lenses.

elements.name: Yttrium
elements.nameMeaning: From Ytterby, a village in Sweden

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Yttrium comes from one tiny Swedish quarry called Ytterby that gave its name to four different elements — a world record for a village. Yttrium makes the red glow in old TV screens and the crystals inside powerful lasers used in surgery.
funFacts: Four elements are named after the same little village: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.
Old color televisions glowed red thanks to a yttrium compound.
YAG lasers made from yttrium crystals cut metal and perform eye surgery.
Yttrium helped make the first superconductor that works in cheap liquid nitrogen.
It was carried to the Moon and back — Apollo samples were studied for it.

compounds.name: Yttrium oxide
compounds.about: The most common yttrium chemical, used in phosphors and ceramics.

compounds.name: YAG
compounds.about: The crystal inside powerful industrial and surgical lasers.

compounds.name: YBCO
compounds.about: A superconductor that works at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

compounds.name: Yttrium oxysulfide
compounds.about: Glowed red in old cathode-ray television tubes.

compounds.name: Yttrium vanadate
compounds.about: A laser crystal used in green laser pointers.

compounds.name: Yttrium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in optical coatings on lenses.

compounds.name: Yttrium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make yttrium metal and other chemicals.

compounds.name: Yttrium iron boride
compounds.about: Related to the strong magnets in headphones.

compounds.name: YIG
compounds.about: A magnetic crystal used in microwave electronics.

compounds.name: Yttria-stabilized zirconia
compounds.about: A tough ceramic used for fake diamonds and dental crowns.

elements.name: Zirconium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Zirconium is a tough silvery metal that shrugs off heat, acid and corrosion, and it lets neutrons pass straight through — which makes it the perfect metal tube to hold nuclear fuel. Its most famous compound, cubic zirconia, sparkles so much it is used as a diamond stand-in.
funFacts: Cubic zirconia looks so like diamond that only an expert can tell them apart.
Nearly all nuclear fuel rods are wrapped in zirconium tubing.
Zircon crystals from Australia are 4.4 billion years old — the oldest bits of Earth ever found.
Zirconium ceramic knives stay sharp far longer than steel ones.
The metal is so safe in the body that it is used in artificial joints.

compounds.name: Zircon
compounds.about: A gemstone mineral whose oldest crystals date the Earth itself.

compounds.name: Zirconia
compounds.about: Cubic zirconia gems, ceramic knives and dental crowns.

compounds.name: Zirconium chloride
compounds.about: A white solid used to make pure zirconium metal.

compounds.name: Zirconium carbide
compounds.about: Survives temperatures over 3,000 °C.

compounds.name: Zirconium diboride
compounds.about: Protects the leading edges of hypersonic aircraft.

compounds.name: Zirconium nitride
compounds.about: A gold-colored hard coating for tools.

compounds.name: Zirconium sulfate
compounds.about: Used in leather tanning.

compounds.name: Zirconium tungstate
compounds.about: Shrinks when heated — very unusual behavior.

compounds.name: Zirconium hydride
compounds.about: Used in nuclear reactors to slow neutrons.

compounds.name: Zirconium hydroxide
compounds.about: Used in gas masks to absorb harmful chemicals.

elements.name: Niobium
elements.nameMeaning: After Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Niobium is a soft gray metal that becomes a superconductor when it gets very cold, carrying electricity with absolutely no loss. That is why niobium wire coils the giant magnets inside MRI scanners and the Large Hadron Collider. It also grows rainbow colors when you pass electricity through it.
funFacts: Niobium jewelry comes in rainbow colors made without any dye — just electricity.
The magnets in MRI scanners are wound with niobium superconducting wire.
The Large Hadron Collider uses tons of niobium to steer particle beams.
It was confused with tantalum for 50 years because the two are so alike.
A pinch of niobium makes pipeline steel much stronger without adding weight.

compounds.name: Niobium pentoxide
compounds.about: Used in special lenses and capacitors.

compounds.name: Columbite
compounds.about: The main niobium ore, part of 'coltan'.

compounds.name: Lithium niobate
compounds.about: Steers laser light in fiber-optic networks.

compounds.name: Niobium carbide
compounds.about: An extremely hard coating for cutting tools.

compounds.name: Niobium-tin
compounds.about: A superconductor for the strongest magnets built.

compounds.name: Niobium-titanium
compounds.about: The superconducting wire in most MRI machines.

compounds.name: Niobium pentachloride
compounds.about: Used to make pure niobium metal.

compounds.name: Niobium nitride
compounds.about: Used in ultra-sensitive light detectors.

compounds.name: Niobium diselenide
compounds.about: A layered crystal studied in nanoscience.

compounds.name: Potassium niobate
compounds.about: Changes laser colors in optical devices.

elements.name: Molybdenum
elements.nameMeaning: From Greek molybdos, 'lead' (it was mistaken for lead)

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of any metal, so it keeps its strength when things get red hot — perfect for jet engines and furnace parts. It is also essential to life: bacteria use molybdenum to pull nitrogen out of the air so plants can grow.
funFacts: Molybdenum does not melt until 2,623 °C.
Its ore is so soft and gray that people mistook it for lead for centuries.
Molybdenum disulfide is slippery like graphite and is used as a dry lubricant.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria need molybdenum, so life on land depends on it.
German tanks in World War I used molybdenum steel armor.

compounds.name: Molybdenite
compounds.about: The main ore, and a super-slippery dry lubricant.

compounds.name: Molybdenum trioxide
compounds.about: A yellow powder used to make the metal and as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Wulfenite
compounds.about: A striking orange crystal mineral.

compounds.name: Sodium molybdate
compounds.about: A fertilizer and a rust inhibitor.

compounds.name: Molybdenum carbide
compounds.about: A very hard material used in cutting tools.

compounds.name: Ammonium molybdate
compounds.about: Used in lab tests to detect phosphates.

compounds.name: Molybdenum disilicide
compounds.about: Heating elements that glow white hot in furnaces.

compounds.name: Molybdenum hexafluoride
compounds.about: A liquid used to lay down metal films on chips.

compounds.name: Molybdenum pentachloride
compounds.about: A dark green solid used in chemical synthesis.

compounds.name: Molybdenum dioxide
compounds.about: A brown solid used as a catalyst.

elements.name: Technetium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Technetium was the first element ever made by humans rather than found in nature — its name literally means 'artificial'. Every atom of it is radioactive, so any that existed when Earth formed has long since decayed away. Today it is a hospital hero, lighting up scans of bones and hearts.
funFacts: Technetium was the first element created artificially, in 1937.
It left a stubborn gap in Mendeleev's table that nobody could fill for 60 years.
About 30 million medical scans a year use technetium-99m.
Its half-life is only 6 hours in medical use, so it leaves the body quickly.
Astronomers have spotted technetium in certain stars, proving stars are still making elements.

compounds.name: Pertechnetate ion
compounds.about: The form injected for medical scans of the thyroid.

compounds.name: Technetium heptoxide
compounds.about: A yellow solid, the highest oxide of technetium.

compounds.name: Technetium dioxide
compounds.about: A black solid formed when technetium is oxidized.

compounds.name: Sodium pertechnetate
compounds.about: The exact chemical used in hospital imaging kits.

compounds.name: Technetium sulfide
compounds.about: Formed when technetium is precipitated from solution.

compounds.name: Technetium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A red-brown solid studied by chemists.

compounds.name: Pertechnetic acid
compounds.about: A strong acid form of technetium.

compounds.name: Technetium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A golden-yellow volatile solid.

compounds.name: Technetium carbonyl
compounds.about: Used to build medical imaging molecules.

compounds.name: Technetium hydride ion
compounds.about: An unusual ion with nine hydrogen atoms attached.

elements.compoundsNote: Technetium is radioactive and made only in reactors and laboratories, so its compounds are studied by specialists rather than used in everyday life.

elements.name: Ruthenium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Ruthenium is one of the rare platinum metals, and just a tiny sprinkle of it makes other metals far tougher. It is a champion at speeding up chemical reactions, and its compounds are being used to build solar cells that soak up sunlight like a plant leaf.
funFacts: Adding 0.1% ruthenium makes titanium a hundred times more resistant to corrosion.
Ruthenium is one of the rarest metals in the Earth's crust.
The tips of some fancy fountain pen nibs are ruthenium alloy.
Ruthenium dyes power experimental solar cells that mimic photosynthesis.
It won a share of the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its role as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Ruthenium dioxide
compounds.about: Conducts electricity; used in tiny resistors in electronics.

compounds.name: Ruthenium tetroxide
compounds.about: A volatile yellow solid used to reveal fingerprints.

compounds.name: Ruthenium chloride
compounds.about: The starting point for most ruthenium chemistry.

compounds.name: Ruthenium bipyridine
compounds.about: Glows orange under light; used in solar cell research.

compounds.name: Strontium ruthenate
compounds.about: A metallic oxide used in electronic devices.

compounds.name: Grubbs catalyst
compounds.about: A Nobel-winning ruthenium tool for building new molecules.

compounds.name: Laurite
compounds.about: The rare mineral in which ruthenium is found.

compounds.name: Triruthenium dodecacarbonyl
compounds.about: An orange cluster compound used in catalysis.

compounds.name: Ruthenium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A dark brown, very reactive solid.

compounds.name: Potassium ruthenate
compounds.about: An orange salt used as an oxidizing agent.

elements.name: Rhodium
elements.nameMeaning: From Greek rhodon, 'rose', for its pink salts

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Rhodium is the most expensive precious metal in the world — often worth many times more than gold. It is brilliantly shiny and never tarnishes, so white gold jewelry is plated with it. Almost all rhodium goes into car exhausts, where it cleans harmful gases out of the fumes.
funFacts: Rhodium has at times been worth more than ten times the price of gold.
Around 80% of all rhodium ends up in car catalytic converters.
Most 'white gold' rings are actually plated with rhodium to look bright white.
It is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust.
Guinness World Records once gave Paul McCartney a rhodium-plated disc.

compounds.name: Rhodium chloride
compounds.about: The most common rhodium chemical, dark red in color.

compounds.name: Rhodium oxide
compounds.about: A gray-black solid used in catalysts.

compounds.name: Wilkinson's catalyst
compounds.about: A famous rhodium tool for adding hydrogen to molecules.

compounds.name: Rhodium dicarbonyl
compounds.about: Used to make many everyday chemicals.

compounds.name: Rhodium acetate
compounds.about: A green dimer used in advanced organic chemistry.

compounds.name: Rhodium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A black, extremely reactive solid.

compounds.name: Sodium hexachlororhodate
compounds.about: Used in rhodium plating baths.

compounds.name: Rhodium sulfide
compounds.about: A catalyst that resists chemical poisoning.

compounds.name: Rhodium hydride
compounds.about: An intermediate step in hydrogen-adding reactions.

compounds.name: Ammonium hexachlororhodate
compounds.about: A step in purifying rhodium from ore.

elements.name: Palladium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Palladium has an amazing party trick: it can soak up 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas, like a metal sponge. It is a superb catalyst, cleaning up car exhaust fumes and helping chemists build medicines. It is named after an asteroid discovered the year before.
funFacts: A block of palladium can absorb 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas.
Palladium is named after Pallas, an asteroid found just a year earlier.
Most gasoline cars have palladium in the exhaust to clean the fumes.
It is used in the tips of spark plugs and in dental crowns.
Palladium chemistry won the 2010 Nobel Prize for building complex molecules.

compounds.name: Palladium chloride
compounds.about: The workhorse of palladium chemistry; also used in plating.

compounds.name: Tetrakis palladium
compounds.about: A Nobel-winning catalyst for joining carbon atoms.

compounds.name: Palladium oxide
compounds.about: A black powder used in exhaust catalysts.

compounds.name: Palladium acetate
compounds.about: A widely used catalyst in making medicines.

compounds.name: Palladium hydride
compounds.about: What forms when palladium soaks up hydrogen.

compounds.name: Sodium tetrachloropalladate
compounds.about: Used in electroplating and catalysis.

compounds.name: Palladium on carbon
compounds.about: Powdered palladium on charcoal, a lab favorite.

compounds.name: Vysotskite
compounds.about: A rare mineral containing palladium.

compounds.name: Palladium fluoride
compounds.about: Unusual because it is magnetic.

compounds.name: Potassium hexachloropalladate
compounds.about: Used to purify palladium from other metals.

elements.name: Silver
elements.nameMeaning: From Old English seolfor; symbol Ag from Latin argentum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element on the periodic table, and it reflects light better too, which is why mirrors are silvered. It also kills bacteria, so it turns up in bandages and sports socks. Silver's only weakness is that it tarnishes black in polluted air.
funFacts: Silver is the best conductor of electricity of any element.
Mirrors work because of a thin silver coating on the back of the glass.
Before digital cameras, every photograph was made using silver compounds.
Silver kills germs, so it is woven into socks and used in wound dressings.
The country Argentina is named after silver — argentum.

compounds.name: Silver nitrate
compounds.about: Stains skin black; used in medicine and photography.

compounds.name: Silver bromide
compounds.about: The light-sensitive crystal in photographic film.

compounds.name: Silver chloride
compounds.about: Turns purple-gray in sunlight; used in sensors.

compounds.name: Silver sulfide
compounds.about: The black tarnish that dulls silver spoons.

compounds.name: Silver oxide
compounds.about: Powers the tiny button batteries in watches.

compounds.name: Silver iodide
compounds.about: Sprayed into clouds to try to make rain.

compounds.name: Silver fluoride
compounds.about: Used by dentists to stop tooth decay spreading.

compounds.name: Silver carbonate
compounds.about: A yellow solid used in chemistry as an oxidizer.

compounds.name: Silver cyanide
compounds.about: Used in silver electroplating baths.

compounds.name: Pyrargyrite
compounds.about: A deep red 'ruby silver' ore mineral.

elements.name: Cadmium
elements.nameMeaning: From cadmia, the Latin name for zinc ore

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Cadmium gave painters some of the most brilliant yellows, oranges and reds ever made — Monet and Van Gogh both used cadmium paints. Unfortunately cadmium is also quite poisonous and builds up in the body, so today its use is carefully controlled.
funFacts: Cadmium yellow and cadmium red are famous artists' paint colors.
Cadmium is toxic and builds up in the body, so it is banned from most products.
Rechargeable NiCd batteries once powered nearly every cordless device.
Cadmium absorbs neutrons, so it is used in nuclear reactor control rods.
Cadmium selenide quantum dots make the pure colors in QLED televisions.

compounds.name: Cadmium sulfide
compounds.about: The brilliant cadmium yellow artists' pigment.

compounds.name: Cadmium selenide
compounds.about: Quantum dots that glow precise colors in TV screens.

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride
compounds.about: Used in a common type of thin-film solar panel.

compounds.name: Cadmium oxide
compounds.about: A brown powder used in electroplating.

compounds.name: Cadmium chloride
compounds.about: Used in photography and dyeing.

compounds.name: Cadmium hydroxide
compounds.about: The electrode material in NiCd batteries.

compounds.name: Cadmium sulfate
compounds.about: Used in standard cells that produce exact voltages.

compounds.name: Otavite
compounds.about: A rare cadmium carbonate mineral.

compounds.name: Cadmium red
compounds.about: The deep red version of the cadmium pigment.

compounds.name: Cadmium zinc telluride
compounds.about: Detects X-rays and gamma rays in scanners.

elements.name: Indium
elements.nameMeaning: From the indigo-blue line in its spectrum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Indium is a soft metal you can scratch with a fingernail, and it screams — a real crackling sound — when you bend it. Its most important job is invisible: a see-through indium coating on your phone screen is what lets the glass sense your finger.
funFacts: Bend a bar of indium and it makes a crackling 'tin cry' sound.
Every touchscreen has a transparent indium layer that senses your finger.
Indium is so soft you can leave a fingerprint in it.
It sticks to glass, so it is used to seal windows in vacuum equipment.
Indium stays soft even at extremely cold temperatures, so it seals space instruments.

compounds.name: Indium tin oxide
compounds.about: The see-through conductor on every touchscreen.

compounds.name: Indium phosphide
compounds.about: Powers the lasers that send data down fiber-optic cables.

compounds.name: Indium arsenide
compounds.about: Used in infrared and night-vision detectors.

compounds.name: Indium gallium nitride
compounds.about: The glowing layer inside blue and white LEDs.

compounds.name: Indium oxide
compounds.about: A yellow powder used in transparent coatings.

compounds.name: Indium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make other indium chemicals.

compounds.name: Indium antimonide
compounds.about: One of the best infrared detector materials.

compounds.name: Copper indium selenide
compounds.about: A flexible thin-film solar material.

compounds.name: Indium hydroxide
compounds.about: A step in refining indium from zinc ore.

compounds.name: Indium sulfide
compounds.about: A yellow-red solid used in solar cell layers.

elements.name: Tin
elements.nameMeaning: From Old English tin; symbol Sn from Latin stannum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Tin changed history: mix a little tin with copper and you get bronze, hard enough for tools and swords, which started the Bronze Age. Today tin coats steel cans to stop food going rusty, and tin solder holds together every circuit board in every gadget you own.
funFacts: The Bronze Age is named after copper mixed with tin.
Bend a bar of tin and it screeches — the famous 'tin cry'.
In freezing cold, tin crumbles into gray powder; this is called tin pest.
'Tin cans' are actually steel with a very thin tin coating inside.
Solder, which joins electronics together, is mostly tin.

compounds.name: Cassiterite
compounds.about: The main tin ore, and a coating on low-energy glass.

compounds.name: Tin(II) chloride
compounds.about: Used to silver mirrors and in dye-making.

compounds.name: Stannous fluoride
compounds.about: The tooth-protecting fluoride in some toothpastes.

compounds.name: Herzenbergite
compounds.about: A dark tin sulfide mineral.

compounds.name: Tin(IV) chloride
compounds.about: A fuming liquid used to coat glass.

compounds.name: Bronze
compounds.about: The copper-tin alloy that started an entire age of history.

compounds.name: Tin(II) oxide
compounds.about: A blue-black powder used in glass making.

compounds.name: Stannite
compounds.about: A tin-bearing ore mineral.

compounds.name: Tributyltin hydride
compounds.about: A lab reagent; related tin compounds once painted ship hulls.

compounds.name: Organotin stabilizers
compounds.about: Added to PVC plastic to stop it breaking down in sunlight.

elements.name: Antimony
elements.nameMeaning: From Greek anti + monos, 'not alone'; symbol Sb from stibium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Antimony has been used for over 5,000 years — ancient Egyptians ground it into kohl, the black eye make-up you see in tomb paintings. Today its main job is stopping fires: antimony compounds are mixed into plastics, mattresses and clothing to slow burning.
funFacts: Ancient Egyptian black eyeliner was made from an antimony mineral.
Antimony expands as it freezes, which made it perfect for sharp printing type.
It is a flame retardant found in mattresses, car seats and children's pajamas.
Antimony is a metalloid — it looks like a shiny metal but is brittle as glass.
Medieval alchemists were fascinated by it and wrote whole books about it.

compounds.name: Stibnite
compounds.about: The main ore, and the ancient Egyptian eye make-up.

compounds.name: Antimony trioxide
compounds.about: The world's most-used flame retardant.

compounds.name: Antimony trichloride
compounds.about: Once called 'butter of antimony' for its greasy look.

compounds.name: Indium antimonide
compounds.about: A superb infrared detector material.

compounds.name: Stibine
compounds.about: A poisonous gas used in the electronics industry.

compounds.name: Antimony pentoxide
compounds.about: A flame retardant and a catalyst.

compounds.name: Lead-antimony alloy
compounds.about: Makes car battery plates strong enough to last.

compounds.name: Antimony telluride
compounds.about: Converts heat into electricity in small coolers.

compounds.name: Tartar emetic
compounds.about: An old and rather brutal medicine.

compounds.name: Antimony pentafluoride
compounds.about: Part of the strongest acid ever made, called a superacid.

elements.name: Tellurium

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.description: Tellurium has an embarrassing side effect: swallow the tiniest speck and your breath smells of garlic for weeks. It is rarer in the crust than gold. Its big modern use is in solar panels and in materials that turn heat straight into electricity.
funFacts: A microscopic amount of tellurium gives you garlic breath for weeks.
Tellurium is rarer in the Earth's crust than gold or platinum.
It is one of the few elements found combined with gold in nature.
Cadmium telluride solar panels are among the cheapest to make.
Named after the Earth, while its cousin selenium is named after the Moon.

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride
compounds.about: A leading thin-film solar panel material.

compounds.name: Bismuth telluride
compounds.about: Turns electricity into cooling in portable fridges.

compounds.name: Tellurium dioxide
compounds.about: Used in special glass that bends sound and light.

compounds.name: Calaverite
compounds.about: A gold ore mineral that also contains tellurium.

compounds.name: Hydrogen telluride
compounds.about: A gas that smells even worse than rotten eggs.

compounds.name: Zinc telluride
compounds.about: Used in solar cells and infrared devices.

compounds.name: Antimony telluride
compounds.about: A thermoelectric material used in coolers.

compounds.name: GST
compounds.about: Stores data on rewritable discs and in phase-change memory.

compounds.name: Tellurium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A white solid used in chemical synthesis.

compounds.name: Lead telluride
compounds.about: Generates electricity from heat in space probes.

elements.name: Iodine

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.description: Iodine is a shiny purple-black solid that does something strange when warmed: it turns straight into a violet gas without ever becoming liquid. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to work, which is why it is added to table salt all over the world.
funFacts: Solid iodine turns directly into a purple gas — a process called sublimation.
Adding iodine to table salt has prevented illness in millions of people.
Iodine turns starch a dramatic blue-black, a classic school science test.
It was discovered by accident while making gunpowder from seaweed ash.
Iodine tincture was used to clean wounds long before modern antiseptics.

compounds.name: Potassium iodide
compounds.about: Added to table salt; also protects the thyroid after nuclear accidents.

compounds.name: Sodium iodide
compounds.about: A crystal that flashes when radiation hits it, used in detectors.

compounds.name: Silver iodide
compounds.about: Used in cloud seeding to encourage rainfall.

compounds.name: Iodine tincture
compounds.about: The brown antiseptic painted on skin before surgery.

compounds.name: Amiodarone
compounds.about: A heart medicine containing iodine.

compounds.name: Thyroxine
compounds.about: The thyroid hormone that controls how fast your body works.

compounds.name: Hydroiodic acid
compounds.about: One of the strongest acids there is.

compounds.name: Nitrogen triiodide
compounds.about: So unstable that a feather's touch makes it bang.

compounds.name: Potassium iodate
compounds.about: Another iodine source added to salt and flour.

compounds.name: Povidone-iodine
compounds.about: The orange-brown surgical scrub used in hospitals.

elements.name: Xenon

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.description: Xenon is the noble gas that broke the rules. Everyone believed noble gases could never form compounds, until 1962 when a chemist made one from xenon and shocked the world. Xenon also makes the dazzling blue-white light in car headlamps and camera flashes.
funFacts: In 1962 xenon proved that noble gases can react after all, rewriting the textbooks.
Xenon headlights and photo flashes give a brilliant daylight-white glow.
Ion engines on spacecraft push xenon out of the back to fly across the solar system.
Xenon can be used as an anesthetic to send patients to sleep.
It is so rare that xenon is only 0.00001% of the air.

compounds.name: Xenon difluoride
compounds.about: The first easy-to-make xenon compound; used to etch silicon.

compounds.name: Xenon tetrafluoride
compounds.about: Beautiful colorless crystals that stunned chemists in 1962.

compounds.name: Xenon hexafluoride
compounds.about: A yellow solid, the highest xenon fluoride.

compounds.name: Xenon trioxide
compounds.about: An explosive white solid — handle with great care.

compounds.name: Xenon tetroxide
compounds.about: So unstable it explodes above −36 °C.

compounds.name: Xenon hexafluoroplatinate
compounds.about: The very first noble gas compound ever made.

compounds.name: Sodium perxenate
compounds.about: One of the most powerful oxidizing agents known.

compounds.name: Xenon oxytetrafluoride
compounds.about: A colorless liquid used in fluorine chemistry.

compounds.name: Xenon chloride
compounds.about: A short-lived molecule that powers excimer lasers for eye surgery.

compounds.name: Xenon hydroxide hydride
compounds.about: A fragile molecule trapped in frozen ice for study.

elements.name: Cesium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Cesium is the most reactive metal of all and one of only a few that melt in a warm room — a lump would turn to golden liquid in your hand, if it were not so dangerous to touch. Cesium atoms keep the world's time: the official length of one second is defined by cesium.
funFacts: The second is officially defined as 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a cesium atom.
Cesium melts at 28 °C, so it would be liquid on a hot day.
It is the most reactive metal — it explodes on contact with water, even ice.
Cesium is soft, gold-colored and one of only three golden metals with copper and gold.
Cesium clocks lose less than a second in 100 million years.

compounds.name: Cesium chloride
compounds.about: Used to spin DNA apart in laboratories.

compounds.name: Cesium carbonate
compounds.about: A useful base in making medicines.

compounds.name: Cesium hydroxide
compounds.about: One of the strongest bases known.

compounds.name: Cesium nitrate
compounds.about: Used in infrared flares that decoy missiles.

compounds.name: Cesium iodide
compounds.about: Flashes when X-rays hit it; used in medical scanners.

compounds.name: Cesium fluoride
compounds.about: A handy source of fluoride in chemistry.

compounds.name: Cesium formate
compounds.about: A very dense liquid used in deep oil drilling.

compounds.name: Cesium oxide
compounds.about: Used to coat surfaces that release electrons easily.

compounds.name: Pollucite
compounds.about: The mineral almost all cesium is mined from.

compounds.name: Cesium sulfate
compounds.about: Used to separate particles by spinning them fast.

elements.name: Barium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Barium is a heavy metal whose salts are mostly poisonous — except one. Barium sulfate will not dissolve at all, so it passes safely through you, and doctors get patients to drink a 'barium meal' so their insides show up clearly on an X-ray.
funFacts: A 'barium meal' is a thick white drink that makes your gut visible on X-rays.
Barium compounds make the green colors in fireworks.
Its name means 'heavy' — barium minerals are noticeably weighty for their size.
Barium is so reactive it must be stored under oil.
Drilling for oil uses huge amounts of barium to weigh down drilling mud.

compounds.name: Barite
compounds.about: The safe 'barium meal' for X-rays, and a drilling mud weight.

compounds.name: Witherite
compounds.about: Used in making glass and ceramics; also rat poison.

compounds.name: Barium chloride
compounds.about: Colors flames green; used in fireworks.

compounds.name: Barium titanate
compounds.about: Generates electricity when squeezed; used in microphones.

compounds.name: Barium oxide
compounds.about: Used to dry gases and in special glass.

compounds.name: Barium nitrate
compounds.about: The green star in firework displays.

compounds.name: Barium ferrite
compounds.about: The ceramic magnets in speakers and fridge magnets.

compounds.name: Barium sulfide
compounds.about: An early glow-in-the-dark material.

compounds.name: Barium hydroxide
compounds.about: A strong base used in chemistry labs.

compounds.name: YBCO
compounds.about: A high-temperature superconductor containing barium.

elements.name: Lanthanum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Lanthanum's name means 'hidden', because it hid inside another element's ore for years before anyone noticed it. It is the first of the fifteen lanthanides, the row that sits below the main table. Lanthanum makes camera lenses sharper and helps hybrid car batteries store energy.
funFacts: Lanthanum gives its name to a whole family of fifteen elements.
Expensive camera lenses contain lanthanum glass, which bends light beautifully.
Hybrid car batteries can hold kilograms of lanthanum.
Despite being called a 'rare earth', it is more common than lead.
Lanthanum compounds help clean up phosphate from lakes and ponds.

compounds.about: Added to glass to make high-quality camera lenses.

compounds.name: Lanthanum nickel

compounds.name: Lanthanum carbonate
compounds.about: A medicine for kidney patients.

compounds.name: Lanthanum aluminate
compounds.about: A base crystal for growing superconductor films.

compounds.name: Lanthanum manganite
compounds.about: Changes resistance in a magnetic field.

compounds.name: Lanthanum oxysulfide
compounds.about: Glows when hit by X-rays, used in scanner screens.

elements.name: Cerium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Cerium is the most common of all the rare earth elements — there is more cerium in the ground than copper. Scratch it and it throws off sparks, which is exactly how the flint in a cigarette lighter works. It also cleans up exhaust fumes and polishes glass to a perfect shine.
funFacts: The sparking 'flint' in a lighter is mostly cerium alloy.
Cerium is more abundant in the crust than copper, tin or lead.
It is named after Ceres, discovered as an asteroid two years before the element.
Cerium oxide is the standard polish for making telescope and phone glass smooth.
It can breathe oxygen in and out, which is why car exhaust catalysts use it.

compounds.name: Cerium oxide
compounds.about: The world's best glass polish; also cleans car exhaust.

compounds.name: Cerium fluoride

compounds.name: Cerium hexaboride
compounds.about: An electron source in powerful microscopes.

compounds.name: Cerium(III) oxide
compounds.about: Used as a catalyst and in self-cleaning ovens.

compounds.name: Mischmetal
compounds.about: A cerium-rich mixture that makes lighter flints spark.

elements.name: Praseodymium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Praseodymium means 'green twin' — for years it was mixed up with neodymium and the pair were thought to be one element called didymium. Its green salts color glass, and welders wear praseodymium goggles that block the fierce yellow glare of hot metal.
funFacts: Welders' and glassblowers' goggles use praseodymium to filter out the glare.
It was separated from its 'twin' neodymium only in 1885.
Praseodymium salts are a lovely apple green.
Mixed with nickel, it is one of the best materials for reaching ultra-low temperatures.
It goes into the powerful magnets in headphones and wind turbines.

elements.name: Neodymium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Neodymium makes the strongest permanent magnets ever invented — a coin-sized one can lift many kilograms and pinch your fingers hard. These magnets are hidden in headphones, phone speakers, hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbines all over the world.
funFacts: Neodymium magnets are so strong that big ones can break bones.
Every pair of headphones and every phone speaker contains a neodymium magnet.
A single wind turbine can hold hundreds of kilograms of neodymium.
Neodymium glass changes color depending on whether it is daylight or lamplight.
Powerful green laser pointers use a neodymium crystal to make their light.

compounds.about: Used in laser and optical coatings.

compounds.about: A step in separating rare earths.

compounds.name: Neodymium nickelate
compounds.about: Switches between conducting and insulating.

compounds.name: Neodymium glass
compounds.about: Used in the world's most powerful fusion research lasers.

elements.name: Promethium
elements.nameMeaning: After Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Promethium is the only lanthanide that is radioactive all the way through, and there is barely any of it on Earth — perhaps half a kilogram in the whole crust at any moment. It glows faintly in the dark and once powered luminous watch dials and tiny long-life batteries.
funFacts: There is thought to be less than a kilogram of natural promethium in the entire Earth's crust.
It is named after Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humankind.
Promethium glows with a pale blue-green light in the dark.
It was used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials before safer materials took over.
Tiny promethium batteries powered pacemakers and space instruments for years.

elements.name: Samarium
elements.nameMeaning: After the mineral samarskite, named for a Russian official

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Samarium makes magnets that keep working when things get very hot — up to 350 °C, far beyond what other magnets can handle. That is why they sit inside jet engines, electric guitar pickups and precision motors. Samarium was the first element named after a living person.
funFacts: Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength at temperatures that ruin other magnets.
It was the first element ever named after a person who was still alive.
Electric guitar pickups often use samarium magnets for a distinctive sound.
Samarium soaks up neutrons, so it helps control nuclear reactors.
Scientists use samarium-neodymium dating to measure the age of rocks and meteorites.

elements.name: Europium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Europium is the anti-forgery element. Euro banknotes contain europium compounds that glow red and blue under ultraviolet light, which is how cashiers spot fakes. Europium also made the red glow in old television screens and helps make white LED bulbs look warm.
funFacts: Shine UV light on a euro note and europium makes it glow — a hidden security check.
Europium gave old color TVs their bright red.
It is the most reactive of all the lanthanides, tarnishing quickly in air.
Europium is the softest rare earth — about as soft as lead.
Warm-white LED bulbs use europium phosphors to soften the harsh blue light.

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Gadolinium is a superstar in hospitals: injected before an MRI scan, it makes blood vessels and tumours light up brightly so doctors can see them clearly. It is also the champion neutron absorber, and it has the strange ability to warm up when placed in a magnetic field.
funFacts: Gadolinium injections make MRI scans much easier for doctors to read.
It absorbs neutrons better than any other element, so it shields nuclear reactors.
Gadolinium is magnetic, but only when it is cooler than about 20 °C.
Placing gadolinium in a magnetic field makes it heat up — a possible future fridge technology.
It is named after Johan Gadolin, who started the whole rare-earth story.

elements.name: Terbium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Terbium glows a beautiful green, so it makes the green pixels in screens and the green in energy-saving light bulbs. It also does something remarkable: an alloy containing terbium changes shape in a magnetic field, which turns any flat surface into a loudspeaker.
funFacts: Terbium provides the green in fluorescent lamps and older TV screens.
Terfenol-D, a terbium alloy, stretches in a magnetic field and can turn a table into a speaker.

elements.name: Dysprosium

Adding dysprosium keeps electric car magnets working when the motor gets hot.
It has one of the strongest magnetic pulls of any element at low temperatures.
Dysprosium is considered one of the most at-risk 'critical' elements for green technology.
It is used in the control rods that keep nuclear reactors steady.

elements.name: Holmium

elements.description: Holmium is the most magnetic element there is — it can be magnetized more strongly than iron. Because of that it sits inside the strongest laboratory magnets to concentrate their field. Holmium lasers are also used by surgeons to break up kidney stones without cutting.
funFacts: Holmium has the highest magnetic strength of any element.
Holmium lasers zap kidney stones into sand-sized pieces inside the body.

Scientists use holmium glass as a color standard to calibrate instruments.

elements.name: Erbium

elements.description: Erbium keeps the internet running. Every few dozen kilometers along the fiber-optic cables crossing the ocean floor sits a short length of erbium-doped glass that boosts the fading light signal back to full strength — without it, long-distance internet would not work.
funFacts: Erbium amplifiers keep internet signals strong across entire oceans.
Erbium turns glass and crystals a lovely pink color.
Erbium lasers are gentle on water-rich tissue, so dentists and skin doctors use them.

Erbium is added to sunglasses to give a pink tint.
