compounds.name: Erbium sulfate
compounds.about: A pink salt used in laboratory work.

compounds.name: Erbium nitride
compounds.about: Studied for use in electronics.

compounds.name: Erbium hydride
compounds.about: Absorbs hydrogen; used in research targets.

compounds.name: Erbium carbonate
compounds.about: Used in the separation of rare earths.

elements.name: Thulium
elements.nameMeaning: From Thule, an ancient name for the far north

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Thulium is the rarest of the naturally occurring lanthanides, which makes it expensive. Its clever trick is being small: a pea-sized thulium X-ray source can go anywhere, letting doctors and engineers take X-rays in places a big machine could never reach.
funFacts: Thulium is the least abundant lanthanide found in nature.
Portable thulium X-ray units can be carried into the field.
It is named after Thule, the mysterious far-northern land of ancient legend.
Thulium lasers are used in surgery because they are absorbed strongly by water.
Euro banknotes glow blue under UV light partly thanks to thulium.

compounds.name: Thulium oxide
compounds.about: The main compound, used to make the metal and phosphors.

compounds.name: Thulium YAG
compounds.about: A surgical laser crystal.

compounds.name: Thulium chloride
compounds.about: Yellow crystals used in research.

compounds.name: Thulium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in optical coatings.

compounds.name: Thulium nitrate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used to make other compounds.

compounds.name: Thulium sulfate
compounds.about: A green salt used in laboratories.

compounds.name: Thulium iodide
compounds.about: Used in high-intensity lamps.

compounds.name: Thulium hexaboride
compounds.about: A hard material studied for electronics.

compounds.name: Thulium nitride
compounds.about: A magnetic compound studied in research.

compounds.name: Thulium carbonate
compounds.about: Used in rare earth separation.

elements.name: Ytterbium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Ytterbium has a party trick that engineers love: squeeze it and its electrical resistance shoots up. That makes it a perfect sensor for measuring the shock of earthquakes and explosions. Ytterbium atomic clocks are now even more accurate than cesium ones.
funFacts: Ytterbium clocks are so precise they would not lose a second in the age of the universe.
Squeeze ytterbium and it resists electricity more, making it a great pressure sensor.
It is another of the four elements named after Ytterby, Sweden.
Ytterbium fiber lasers cut through thick steel in factories.
It is one of the few lanthanides that is happy in a +2 charge as well as +3.

compounds.name: Ytterbium oxide
compounds.about: Used in lasers, ceramics and as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Ytterbium YAG
compounds.about: The crystal in powerful industrial cutting lasers.

compounds.name: Ytterbium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make ytterbium metal and other compounds.

compounds.name: Ytterbium fluoride
compounds.about: Added to dental fillings so they show on X-rays.

compounds.name: Ytterbium triflate
compounds.about: A catalyst that works even in water.

compounds.name: Ytterbium sulfate
compounds.about: A colorless salt used in laboratories.

compounds.name: Ytterbium hexaboride
compounds.about: Studied as an unusual electronic material.

compounds.name: Ytterbium nitrate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used in materials research.

compounds.name: Ytterbium hydride
compounds.about: Absorbs hydrogen gas readily.

compounds.name: Ytterbium carbonate
compounds.about: Used in separating rare earth elements.

elements.name: Lutetium

discovered.by: Georges Urbain and Carl Auer von Welsbach

elements.nameMeaning: From Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Lutetium is the last and the toughest of the lanthanides — the hardest and densest of the family. It was also the last of them to be discovered, after a bitter argument between chemists in three countries over who found it first and what to call it.
funFacts: Lutetium was the final lanthanide discovered, in 1907.
Three chemists claimed it at once, sparking a famous naming argument.
It is named after Lutetia, the Roman name for the city of Paris.
Lutetium crystals detect gamma rays in PET scanners that find cancer.
It is the hardest and heaviest of all the lanthanides.

compounds.name: LSO
compounds.about: The crystal that detects signals inside PET body scanners.

compounds.name: Lutetium oxide
compounds.about: Used in special glass, ceramics and catalysts.

compounds.name: Lutetium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make lutetium metal.

compounds.name: LuAG
compounds.about: A crystal used in scanners and lasers.

compounds.name: Lutetium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in optical coatings.

compounds.name: Lutetium-177 therapy
compounds.about: A radioactive medicine that targets and kills tumours.

compounds.name: Lutetium nitrate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used in research.

compounds.name: Lutetium sulfate
compounds.about: A colorless salt used in laboratories.

compounds.name: Lutetium tantalate
compounds.about: One of the densest white materials known; used in X-ray screens.

compounds.name: Lutetium phosphate
compounds.about: A very stable compound studied by chemists.

elements.name: Hafnium

discovered.by: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Hafnium is zirconium's near-identical twin — so alike that it took until 1923 to tell them apart. But in one way they are opposites: hafnium gobbles up neutrons while zirconium lets them pass, so submarines use hafnium control rods to switch reactors on and off.
funFacts: Hafnium and zirconium are so chemically similar they are extremely hard to separate.
Nuclear submarine reactors are controlled with hafnium rods.
Hafnium oxide made modern computer chips possible by replacing an older insulator.
Hafnium carbide has one of the highest melting points of any material, near 3,900 °C.
It is named after Copenhagen, where it was finally discovered.

compounds.name: Hafnium oxide
compounds.about: The insulating layer that keeps modern chips from leaking power.

compounds.name: Hafnium carbide
compounds.about: Melts at nearly 3,900 °C, one of the highest ever measured.

compounds.name: Hafnium chloride
compounds.about: A white solid used to make hafnium metal and chip coatings.

compounds.name: Hafnium nitride
compounds.about: A very hard, heat-resistant coating.

compounds.name: Hafnium diboride
compounds.about: Protects spacecraft edges from re-entry heat.

compounds.name: Hafnon
compounds.about: A rare mineral containing hafnium.

compounds.name: Hafnium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in special infrared glasses.

compounds.name: Hafnium hydride
compounds.about: Used in some nuclear applications.

compounds.name: Hafnium iodide
compounds.about: Used to make ultra-pure hafnium metal.

compounds.name: Hafnium tantalum carbide
compounds.about: Long held the record for highest melting point.

elements.name: Tantalum
elements.nameMeaning: After Tantalus of Greek myth, who could never drink

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Tantalum is almost impossible to corrode — acids barely touch it — and it stores electricity brilliantly in tiny spaces. That is why a small tantalum capacitor sits in nearly every cell phone. It is also safe in the human body, so surgeons use it for plates and implants.
funFacts: Nearly every cell phone contains a tiny tantalum capacitor.
Named after Tantalus, who stood in water he could never drink — because tantalum refuses to absorb acid.
Tantalum does not react with body fluids, so it is used for skull plates.
Its ore, coltan, is mined in conflict zones, making sourcing an ethical issue.
Tantalum melts at 3,017 °C, one of the highest of all metals.

compounds.name: Tantalum pentoxide
compounds.about: The insulator inside the capacitors in your phone.

compounds.name: Tantalite
compounds.about: The ore mineral, part of 'coltan'.

compounds.name: Tantalum carbide
compounds.about: Extremely hard; used on cutting tools.

compounds.name: Lithium tantalate
compounds.about: Used in cell phone signal filters and infrared sensors.

compounds.name: Tantalum pentachloride
compounds.about: Used to make tantalum metal and coatings.

compounds.name: Tantalum nitride
compounds.about: A thin film used in computer chip wiring.

compounds.name: Tantalum diboride
compounds.about: A hard ceramic resistant to heat.

compounds.name: Tantalum pentafluoride
compounds.about: A strong acid catalyst.

compounds.name: Tantalum silicide
compounds.about: Used in chip manufacturing.

compounds.name: Tantalum hafnium carbide
compounds.about: Among the most heat-resistant materials known.

elements.name: Tungsten
elements.nameMeaning: From Swedish tung sten, 'heavy stone'; symbol W from wolfram

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Tungsten is the champion of heat: it melts at 3,422 °C, higher than any other metal on the table. That is why old light bulbs glowed with a thin tungsten wire. It is also incredibly dense — a tungsten cube feels shockingly heavy for its size, almost like gold.
funFacts: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal: 3,422 °C.
Old-fashioned light bulbs glowed because a tungsten filament got white hot.
Tungsten is nearly as dense as gold, so it makes fake gold bars and darts.
Tungsten carbide is so hard it is used to drill through rock and cut steel.
It is the only metal that some bacteria use in their enzymes.

compounds.name: Tungsten carbide
compounds.about: Nearly as hard as diamond; drill bits, saw tips and jewelry.

compounds.name: Scheelite
compounds.about: A tungsten ore that glows bright blue under UV light.

compounds.name: Wolframite
compounds.about: The other main tungsten ore, giving the symbol W.

compounds.name: Tungsten trioxide
compounds.about: Used in smart windows that darken at the touch of a button.

compounds.name: Tungsten disulfide
compounds.about: A slippery dry lubricant that works in space.

compounds.name: Sodium tungstate
compounds.about: Used to make fireproof fabrics.

compounds.name: Tungsten hexafluoride
compounds.about: One of the heaviest gases; used to make computer chips.

compounds.name: Tungsten hexachloride
compounds.about: Dark blue crystals used as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Phosphotungstic acid
compounds.about: A stain used to see viruses under a microscope.

compounds.name: Tungsten boride
compounds.about: An extremely hard material studied as a diamond substitute.

elements.name: Rhenium
elements.nameMeaning: From Rhenus, Latin for the river Rhine

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Rhenium was the very last stable element to be discovered, in 1925 — every element found since then has been radioactive. It is one of the rarest things in the crust, and it has the second-highest melting point of all metals. Jet engine blades depend on it.
funFacts: Rhenium was the last stable element ever discovered on Earth.
The hottest parts of jet engine turbine blades contain rhenium.
It is one of the ten rarest elements in the Earth's crust.
Rhenium keeps its strength at temperatures that would melt most metals.
There is a volcano in Russia that puffs out pure rhenium sulfide.

compounds.name: Rhenium heptoxide
compounds.about: A yellow solid used to make catalysts.

compounds.name: Rhenium disulfide
compounds.about: A layered crystal studied in nanoscience.

compounds.name: Perrhenic acid
compounds.about: The usual soluble form used in industry.

compounds.name: Ammonium perrhenate
compounds.about: The main traded rhenium chemical.

compounds.name: Rhenium trichloride
compounds.about: A dark red solid with unusual triangle-shaped clusters.

compounds.name: Rhenium trioxide
compounds.about: A red solid that conducts electricity like copper.

compounds.name: Rhenium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A yellow liquid used in coating processes.

compounds.name: Dirhenium decacarbonyl
compounds.about: A white solid used in catalysis research.

compounds.name: Rhenium diboride
compounds.about: Hard enough to scratch diamond in some tests.

compounds.name: Rhenium silicide
compounds.about: Studied for turning heat into electricity.

elements.name: Osmium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Osmium is the densest element in the universe — a soccer-ball-sized lump would weigh as much as a small car. Its name means 'smell', because one of its compounds gives off a sharp, dangerous odor. Tiny osmium tips make fountain pen nibs and record player needles last for years.
funFacts: Osmium is the densest natural element; a cubic centimeter weighs 22.6 grams.
Its name means 'smell' because osmium tetroxide has a nasty sharp odor.
A blue-gray metal, it is one of the few that is not silver or gray-white.
Osmium tips on fountain pens and record needles resist wear for decades.
It is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust.

compounds.name: Osmium tetroxide
compounds.about: Stains biological samples black so they show under microscopes.

compounds.name: Osmium trichloride
compounds.about: A dark solid used to make other osmium compounds.

compounds.name: Erlichmanite
compounds.about: A rare mineral containing osmium.

compounds.name: Potassium osmate
compounds.about: A safer, easier-to-handle source of osmium in chemistry.

compounds.name: Osmium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A yellow, very reactive solid.

compounds.name: Triosmium dodecacarbonyl
compounds.about: A yellow cluster studied in catalysis.

compounds.name: Osmium dioxide
compounds.about: A brown solid that conducts electricity.

compounds.name: Osmiridium
compounds.about: A natural alloy used for hard-wearing pen tips.

compounds.name: Osmium diboride
compounds.about: An extremely hard material studied by scientists.

compounds.name: Sodium osmate
compounds.about: Used in chemistry to add oxygen atoms to molecules.

elements.name: Iridium
elements.nameMeaning: From Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal known — nothing on Earth can rust it. It is also the clue that solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: a thin layer of iridium in rocks worldwide proved that a giant asteroid struck Earth and wiped out the dinosaurs.
funFacts: A worldwide layer of iridium in the rocks is the evidence for the dinosaur-killing asteroid.
Iridium is rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids.
It is the most corrosion-resistant metal — even acid mixtures cannot touch it.
The official kilogram was once a platinum-iridium cylinder kept in Paris.
Iridium spark plugs last far longer than ordinary ones.

compounds.name: Iridium trichloride
compounds.about: The starting point for most iridium chemistry.

compounds.name: Iridium dioxide
compounds.about: Used in electrodes that split water into hydrogen.

compounds.name: Iridium complex
compounds.about: Glows brightly; used in OLED phone and TV screens.

compounds.name: Iridium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A yellow, extremely reactive solid.

compounds.name: Chloroiridic acid
compounds.about: Used in plating and catalyst making.

compounds.name: Vaska's complex
compounds.about: A famous molecule that taught chemists how catalysts work.

compounds.name: Iridium sulfide
compounds.about: A rare mineral form of iridium.

compounds.name: Iridium carbonyl
compounds.about: A yellow cluster used in catalysis research.

compounds.name: Strontium iridate
compounds.about: Studied for unusual magnetic and electronic behavior.

compounds.name: Platinum-iridium
compounds.about: The alloy of the old standard kilogram and meter bars.

elements.name: Platinum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Platinum is rarer than gold and does not tarnish, which is why it is prized for jewelry. But its real superpower is chemistry: platinum speeds up reactions without being used up. It cleans car exhausts, helps make fertilizer, and a platinum drug fights cancer.
funFacts: All the platinum ever mined would fit in an average living room.
Spanish explorers threw platinum away, calling it annoying 'little silver'.
Platinum in car exhausts turns poisonous gases into harmless ones.
Cisplatin, a platinum medicine, cures most cases of testicular cancer.
A 'platinum record' award is more valuable than gold — just like the metal.

compounds.name: Cisplatin
compounds.about: One of the most successful cancer medicines ever made.

compounds.name: Chloroplatinic acid
compounds.about: Used to make catalysts and for plating.

compounds.name: Adams' catalyst
compounds.about: A brown powder chemists use to add hydrogen to molecules.

compounds.name: Platinum dichloride
compounds.about: Used to prepare other platinum compounds.

compounds.name: Cooperite
compounds.about: The main mineral platinum is mined from.

compounds.name: Platinum hexafluoride
compounds.about: So greedy for electrons it made the first noble gas compound.

compounds.name: Karstedt's catalyst
compounds.about: Used to cure silicone rubber for molds and seals.

compounds.name: Platinum on carbon
compounds.about: The catalyst inside hydrogen fuel cells.

compounds.name: Potassium tetrachloroplatinate
compounds.about: A red salt used to make cisplatin.

compounds.name: Sperrylite
compounds.about: A silvery mineral and important platinum ore.

elements.name: Gold
elements.nameMeaning: From Old English gold; symbol Au from Latin aurum

zhRadical.note: The 金 (gold/metal) radical — gold is the character all metal names are built from.

elements.description: Gold never rusts, never tarnishes and never fades — a gold mask buried for 3,000 years comes out as bright as the day it was made. That permanence, plus its warm yellow shine, has made it precious in every culture on Earth. It is also astonishingly bendy.
funFacts: One gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet a whole square meter in size.
All the gold ever mined would form a cube only about 22 meters on each side.
Gold is made when neutron stars crash into each other in space.
Astronauts' visors have a whisper-thin gold layer to reflect harmful sunlight.
Gold is edible — gold leaf decorates fancy desserts and passes right through you.

compounds.name: Chloroauric acid
compounds.about: The dissolved form used for plating and making gold nanoparticles.

compounds.name: Gold(III) chloride
compounds.about: Red crystals used to make ruby-red stained glass.

compounds.name: Gold(III) oxide
compounds.about: The most stable oxide of gold, a brown solid.

compounds.name: Calaverite
compounds.about: One of the few minerals where gold is chemically combined.

compounds.name: Potassium dicyanoaurate
compounds.about: Used in gold electroplating baths.

compounds.name: Gold(I) chloride
compounds.about: A yellow solid used in chemistry research.

compounds.name: Gold sulfide
compounds.about: A rare compound studied by chemists.

compounds.name: Auranofin
compounds.about: A gold medicine used to treat arthritis.

compounds.name: Aurostibite
compounds.about: A rare gold-antimony mineral.

compounds.name: Purple of Cassius
compounds.about: Gold nanoparticles that turn glass a deep ruby red.

elements.name: Mercury
elements.nameMeaning: After the planet Mercury; symbol Hg from Greek hydrargyros, 'water silver'

zhRadical.note: The 水 (water) radical — mercury is a liquid.

elements.description: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature — a shimmering silver puddle that rolls into perfect beads. For centuries it filled thermometers and barometers, but mercury is a serious poison, so today it is being replaced almost everywhere.
funFacts: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
It is so dense that an iron cannonball floats on it.
'Mad as a hatter' comes from hat makers who were poisoned by mercury fumes.
Mercury was once used in thermometers, but safer liquids have replaced it.
The planet, the metal and the Roman messenger god all share the same name.

compounds.name: Cinnabar
compounds.about: A brilliant red mineral, the main mercury ore and the pigment vermilion.

compounds.name: Mercury(II) chloride
compounds.about: Very poisonous; once used as a disinfectant.

compounds.name: Calomel
compounds.about: Used in old electrical reference cells and old medicines.

compounds.name: Mercury(II) oxide
compounds.about: Heating it releases oxygen — how oxygen was discovered.

compounds.name: Methylmercury
compounds.about: The dangerous form that builds up in fish.

compounds.name: Mercury fulminate
compounds.about: An explosive once used in the caps of bullets.

compounds.name: Mercury(II) iodide
compounds.about: Changes color from red to yellow when heated.

compounds.name: Dental amalgam
compounds.about: The old silver-colored tooth fillings.

compounds.name: Mercury selenide
compounds.about: Studied for infrared detectors.

compounds.name: Thiomersal
compounds.about: A mercury preservative once used in some vaccines.

elements.name: Thallium
elements.nameMeaning: From Greek thallos, 'green shoot', for its green spectral line

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Thallium has a grim nickname: 'the poisoner's poison'. It has no taste, no smell, and its effects look like ordinary illness, so it featured in many famous crime stories. Handled safely, though, thallium helps doctors take pictures of the heart and lets night-vision lenses see in the dark.
funFacts: Thallium is tasteless and odorless, which made it a notorious murder weapon in fiction and fact.
Agatha Christie used thallium in a novel so accurately that it later helped doctors save a child.
It was discovered by its bright green line in a spectroscope.
Thallium is so soft you can cut it with a knife and mark paper with it.
Doctors once used a thallium scan to check blood flow to the heart.

compounds.name: Thallium sulfate
compounds.about: Once sold as rat poison, now banned in most countries.

compounds.name: KRS-5
compounds.about: A crystal used in infrared spectroscopy and night vision.

compounds.name: Thallium oxide
compounds.about: Used in special high-refraction glass.

compounds.name: Thallium chloride
compounds.about: A white solid used in chemistry and medical imaging.

compounds.name: Thallium-doped sodium iodide
compounds.about: The crystal that flashes when radiation passes through detectors.

compounds.name: Thallium carbonate
compounds.about: Used to make artificial gemstones and glass.

compounds.name: Thallium superconductor
compounds.about: One of the highest-temperature superconductors known.

compounds.name: Thallium nitrate
compounds.about: Burns green in fireworks and flares.

compounds.name: Thallium sulfide
compounds.about: Changes conductivity in infrared light; used in detectors.

compounds.name: Thallium hydroxide
compounds.about: A strong base used in laboratories.

elements.name: Lead
elements.nameMeaning: From Old English lead; symbol Pb from Latin plumbum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Lead is heavy, soft and easy to shape, so the Romans made water pipes out of it — the word 'plumber' comes from the Latin for lead. Sadly lead is poisonous, especially for children, so it has been removed from paint, gasoline and pipes. It is still the best shield against X-rays.
funFacts: The word 'plumbing' comes from plumbum, the Latin name for lead.
Lead aprons at the dentist stop X-rays from reaching the rest of your body.
Removing lead from gasoline made the air in cities dramatically cleaner.
Pencil 'lead' contains no lead at all — it is graphite, a form of carbon.
Every car battery is built from lead plates soaking in acid.

compounds.name: Galena
compounds.about: The shiny gray main ore of lead, often containing silver too.

compounds.name: Lead dioxide
compounds.about: The positive plate inside every car battery.

compounds.name: Lead chromate
compounds.about: 'Chrome yellow' — the old school-bus and road-marking paint.

compounds.name: Lead sulfate
compounds.about: Forms on battery plates as they discharge.

compounds.name: Cerussite
compounds.about: 'White lead' — the old paint pigment now banned as toxic.

compounds.name: Red lead
compounds.about: A bright orange-red rust-proof paint primer.

compounds.name: Lead telluride
compounds.about: Turns heat into electricity in deep-space probes.

compounds.name: Litharge
compounds.about: Used to make crystal glass sparkle.

compounds.name: PZT
compounds.about: Makes ultrasound scanners and sonar work by vibrating.

compounds.name: Lead azide
compounds.about: A sensitive explosive used in detonators.

elements.name: Bismuth

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Bismuth grows the most beautiful crystals in the whole periodic table: rainbow-colored stair-stepped staircases that look like something from a video game. It is a heavy metal that is remarkably safe — it is the pink medicine you take for an upset tummy.
funFacts: Bismuth crystals form rainbow-colored spiral staircases you can grow at home.
It is the heaviest element that is safe enough to swallow as medicine.
Bismuth is technically radioactive, but its half-life is a billion times the age of the universe.
Like water and gallium, bismuth expands when it freezes.
It is the most strongly diamagnetic element — it is pushed away by magnets.

compounds.name: Bismuth subsalicylate
compounds.about: The pink stomach medicine for indigestion.

compounds.name: Bismuthinite
compounds.about: The main ore mineral of bismuth.

compounds.name: Bismuth oxide
compounds.about: Used in ceramics, glass and fireproofing.

compounds.name: Bismuth oxychloride
compounds.about: The pearly shimmer in nail polish and make-up.

compounds.name: Bismuth telluride
compounds.about: Powers small electric coolers and camping fridges.

compounds.name: Bismuth nitrate
compounds.about: Used to make other bismuth compounds and pigments.

compounds.name: Bismuth vanadate
compounds.about: A bright yellow pigment replacing toxic lead chrome.

compounds.name: BSCCO
compounds.about: A high-temperature superconductor made into wire.

compounds.name: Bismuth subcarbonate
compounds.about: Used in stomach medicines and cosmetics.

compounds.name: Wood's metal
compounds.about: A bismuth alloy that melts in hot water; used in fire sprinklers.

elements.name: Polonium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Polonium was discovered by Marie Curie, who named it after Poland, the country she came from, to draw attention to its struggle for independence. It is intensely radioactive — a single gram gives off so much energy that it glows blue and heats itself to 500 °C.
funFacts: Marie Curie named polonium after her homeland, Poland.
A gram of polonium gets hot enough to glow — it heats itself to about 500 °C.
Polonium is roughly 250,000 times more toxic than cyanide.
It powered the heaters that kept Soviet Moon rovers warm through the freezing lunar night.
It was the first element the Curies discovered, months before radium.

compounds.name: Polonium dioxide
compounds.about: The most stable oxide, a pale yellow solid.

compounds.name: Polonium dichloride
compounds.about: A dark red solid studied in tiny amounts.

compounds.name: Polonium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A yellow solid used in polonium chemistry.

compounds.name: Polonium hydride
compounds.about: An unstable gas, the heaviest relative of water.

compounds.name: Polonium dibromide
compounds.about: A purple-brown solid made in trace amounts.

compounds.name: Polonium trioxide
compounds.about: A rare higher oxide of polonium.

compounds.name: Polonium sulfide
compounds.about: A black solid that barely dissolves in water.

compounds.name: Sodium polonite
compounds.about: A salt formed with strong alkali.

compounds.name: Polonium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A volatile compound predicted and briefly studied.

compounds.name: Polonium metal
compounds.about: The pure element, used as a heat source in spacecraft.

elements.compoundsNote: Polonium is so radioactive and rare that its compounds exist only in specialist laboratories, studied in microscopic quantities.

elements.name: Astatine

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.description: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth — scientists estimate that the entire planet's crust holds less than a teaspoonful at any moment. Nobody has ever seen a visible piece of it, because it is so radioactive it would vaporize itself from its own heat.
funFacts: There is less than 30 grams of astatine in the whole Earth's crust at any time.
No one has ever seen astatine — a visible lump would boil away from its own radioactivity.
Its name means 'unstable', which is exactly right.
Astatine-211 is being tested as a precision cancer treatment.
It is the heaviest of the halogens, the family that includes chlorine and iodine.

compounds.name: Hydrogen astatide
compounds.about: The astatine version of hydrochloric acid.

compounds.name: Sodium astatide
compounds.about: The salt form, like sodium chloride.

compounds.name: Astatine iodide
compounds.about: A mixed halogen molecule detected in trace studies.

compounds.name: Astatine bromide
compounds.about: Another interhalogen studied in solution.

compounds.name: Astatine chloride
compounds.about: Formed when astatine meets chlorine.

compounds.name: Astatite ion
compounds.about: An oxidized form found in water solutions.

compounds.name: Astatate ion
compounds.about: A higher oxidized form, like iodate.

compounds.name: Diastatine
compounds.about: The predicted pure molecule; never actually observed.

compounds.name: Astatine cancer agent
compounds.about: An experimental molecule that carries astatine to tumours.

compounds.name: Methyl astatide
compounds.about: An organic astatine compound made in trace amounts.

elements.compoundsNote: Astatine is so rare and short-lived that its chemistry is worked out from a handful of atoms at a time — most of these compounds are known only from tracer experiments.

elements.name: Radon
elements.nameMeaning: From radium, the element it comes from

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.description: Radon is a noble gas that is also radioactive. It seeps invisibly out of the ground from uranium in rocks and can build up inside houses, which is why many homes are tested for it. It is the heaviest gas on the periodic table.
funFacts: Radon is the heaviest gas known — about eight times denser than air.
It leaks naturally out of soil and rock, and can collect in basements.
Radon is the second biggest cause of lung cancer after smoking, so homes are tested for it.
It glows a beautiful yellow-orange when cooled into a solid.
Radon is made continuously as uranium in the ground slowly decays.

compounds.name: Radon difluoride
compounds.about: The one compound that has actually been made and observed.

elements.compoundsNote: Radon is a noble gas and intensely radioactive, so almost no chemistry has been done with it. Radon difluoride is essentially the only compound ever confirmed.

elements.name: Francium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Francium is the second rarest element in the Earth's crust — there may be only about 30 grams of it on the whole planet at any moment. It falls apart in about 22 minutes, so nobody has ever collected enough to see. It was the last element to be found in nature.
funFacts: Francium was the last element ever discovered in nature, in 1939.
It was found by Marguerite Perey, who later became the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences.
A francium atom lasts only about 22 minutes before falling apart.
The largest amount ever gathered was about 300,000 atoms — far too few to see.
It would be the most reactive metal of all, if you could ever get enough to test.

compounds.name: Francium chloride
compounds.about: The salt form, studied with only a few thousand atoms.

compounds.name: Francium hydroxide
compounds.about: Predicted to be the strongest base of any element.

compounds.name: Francium carbonate
compounds.about: Detected in trace chemistry experiments.

compounds.name: Francium nitrate

compounds.name: Francium sulfate

compounds.name: Francium perchlorate
compounds.about: Used in trace experiments to separate francium.

compounds.name: Francium iodide
compounds.about: Predicted from the pattern of the other alkali metals.

compounds.name: Francium fluoride
compounds.about: The fluoride salt, known only by prediction.

compounds.name: Francium superoxide
compounds.about: Expected to form when francium meets oxygen.

compounds.name: Francium hydride
compounds.about: A predicted compound with hydrogen.

elements.compoundsNote: Francium exists only as a handful of atoms at a time, so its compounds are mostly predicted from the behavior of cesium rather than made in a bottle.

elements.name: Radium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Radium glows in the dark with an eerie blue-green light, and when Marie Curie discovered it people thought it was magical. It was put in toothpaste, chocolate and glowing watch dials — until it became tragically clear how dangerous its radiation really is.
funFacts: Marie Curie processed tons of ore by hand to extract a tiny speck of radium.
Radium glows blue-green in the dark all by itself.
Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead boxes.
The 'Radium Girls' who painted watch dials became terribly ill, changing worker safety laws forever.
Radium was once added to toothpaste and face cream as a health fad.

compounds.name: Radium chloride
compounds.about: The first radium compound Marie Curie purified.

compounds.name: Radium bromide
compounds.about: Glows so brightly it lit up the Curies' laboratory at night.

compounds.name: Radium sulfate
compounds.about: One of the least soluble sulfates known.

compounds.name: Radium carbonate
compounds.about: Formed when radium salts meet carbonate.

compounds.name: Radium nitrate
compounds.about: Used in early radium purification.

compounds.name: Radium oxide
compounds.about: Formed when radium metal meets air.

compounds.name: Radium-223 therapy
compounds.about: A modern medicine that targets cancer that has spread to bone.

compounds.name: Radium fluoride
compounds.about: An insoluble salt studied in the laboratory.

compounds.name: Radium hydroxide
compounds.about: The most soluble hydroxide of its family.

compounds.name: Radium sulfide
compounds.about: A compound studied in early radiochemistry.

elements.name: Actinium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Actinium gives its name to the actinides, the bottom row of the periodic table. It is intensely radioactive — about 150 times more so than radium — and glows an eerie pale blue in the dark. Today it is being used to build very precise cancer treatments.
funFacts: Actinium glows pale blue in the dark from its own radioactivity.
It is around 150 times more radioactive than radium.
The entire actinide row of the periodic table is named after it.
Actinium-225 is used in targeted therapy that destroys cancer cells one at a time.
There is only a tiny fraction of a gram in the Earth's crust at any moment.

compounds.name: Actinium oxide
compounds.about: The most stable common form of actinium.

compounds.name: Actinium chloride
compounds.about: A white solid used in radiochemistry.

compounds.name: Actinium fluoride
compounds.about: An insoluble salt used in purification.

compounds.name: Actinium bromide
compounds.about: A white solid studied by chemists.

compounds.name: Actinium nitrate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used in separations.

compounds.name: Actinium oxalate
compounds.about: Used to precipitate actinium out of solution.

compounds.name: Actinium phosphate
compounds.about: An insoluble compound studied in the laboratory.

compounds.name: Actinium hydride
compounds.about: Formed when actinium reacts with hydrogen.

compounds.name: Actinium oxychloride
compounds.about: Formed when the chloride meets moisture.

compounds.name: Actinium-225 therapy
compounds.about: Attached to antibodies that hunt down cancer cells.

elements.compoundsNote: Actinium is extremely rare and radioactive; its compounds are made only in tiny research quantities.

elements.name: Thorium
elements.nameMeaning: After Thor, the Norse god of thunder

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Thorium is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder. It is radioactive but only very weakly, and it is three times more common than uranium. Many scientists think thorium could one day fuel a safer kind of nuclear reactor that makes far less long-lived waste.
funFacts: Thorium is named after Thor, the hammer-wielding Norse thunder god.
It is about three times more abundant in the Earth's crust than uranium.
Old camping lantern mantles glowed brilliantly thanks to thorium.
Thorium reactors are being researched as a safer future power source.
Its half-life is 14 billion years — longer than the age of the universe.

compounds.name: Thorium dioxide
compounds.about: Has one of the highest melting points of any oxide, 3,300 °C.

compounds.name: Thorite
compounds.about: A thorium ore mineral.

compounds.name: Monazite
compounds.about: The main source of thorium, mined from beach sands.

compounds.name: Thorium fluoride
compounds.about: Used in optical coatings for infrared lenses.

compounds.name: Thorium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make thorium metal.

compounds.name: Thorium nitrate
compounds.about: Used to make the glowing mantles in old gas lamps.

compounds.name: Thorium carbide
compounds.about: Studied as a nuclear fuel material.

compounds.name: Thorium nitride
compounds.about: A hard, heat-resistant nuclear material.

compounds.name: Thorium hexaboride
compounds.about: A very hard, high-melting compound.

compounds.name: Thorium sulfate
compounds.about: A soluble salt used in laboratory separations.

elements.name: Protactinium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Protactinium's name means 'before actinium', because when it decays it turns into actinium. It is one of the rarest and most expensive natural elements — extracting just over 100 grams once took 60 tons of nuclear waste and years of work.
funFacts: Protactinium means 'parent of actinium', because it decays into it.
One famous extraction produced 125 grams from 60 tons of waste.
It is one of the most expensive naturally occurring materials on Earth.
Scientists use protactinium in ocean sediments to study ancient climate.
It is silvery and shiny when fresh, but tarnishes in air.

compounds.about: A yellow solid used to make the metal.

compounds.name: Protactinium hydroxide

compounds.name: Protactinium pentaiodide
compounds.about: Used to purify protactinium metal.

compounds.name: Protactinium nitride
compounds.about: A compound studied by nuclear chemists.

elements.compoundsNote: Protactinium is extraordinarily rare and radioactive, so all of these are laboratory-scale research compounds.

elements.name: Uranium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Uranium is the heaviest element found in useful amounts in nature, and its atoms can be split to release enormous energy. That single fact gave the world nuclear power stations and, darkly, nuclear weapons. Uranium's slow decay is also what keeps the Earth's insides warm.
funFacts: Splitting one kilogram of uranium releases as much energy as burning 3,000 tons of coal.
Uranium's radioactive decay helps keep the Earth's core hot and its volcanoes active.
Antique 'Vaseline glass' contains uranium and glows bright green under UV light.
Uranium was named after the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier.
Geologists date the oldest rocks on Earth by measuring uranium decay.

compounds.name: Uranium dioxide
compounds.about: The black ceramic pellets that fuel nuclear power stations.

compounds.name: Uranyl nitrate
compounds.about: A yellow salt used in processing nuclear fuel.

compounds.name: Uranium hexafluoride
compounds.about: The gas used to separate uranium types for fuel.

compounds.name: Pitchblende

compounds.name: Triuranium octoxide
compounds.about: 'Yellowcake' — the form uranium is traded in.

compounds.name: Carnotite
compounds.about: A bright yellow uranium ore mineral.

compounds.name: Uranium carbide
compounds.about: An advanced nuclear fuel material.

compounds.name: Uranium nitride
compounds.about: A dense fuel studied for future reactors.

compounds.name: Uranium tetrafluoride
compounds.about: 'Green salt' — a step in making reactor fuel.

compounds.name: Uranium glass
compounds.about: Antique glassware that fluoresces bright green under UV.

elements.name: Neptunium
elements.nameMeaning: After the planet Neptune, next after Uranus

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Neptunium was the first element ever made that sits beyond uranium on the periodic table, opening a whole new frontier. It was named after Neptune because that planet comes after Uranus, just as neptunium comes after uranium.
funFacts: Neptunium was the first man-made element heavier than uranium.
The naming follows the planets: uranium, neptunium, then plutonium.
Tiny traces occur naturally in uranium ore.
Neptunium is used in detectors that sense high-energy neutrons.
Its discovery earned Edwin McMillan a share of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

compounds.name: Neptunium carbide
compounds.about: A research material for reactor fuel.

compounds.about: A green solid made in small amounts.

compounds.name: Neptunyl hydroxide
compounds.about: Important in studies of nuclear waste in groundwater.

elements.compoundsNote: Neptunium is a synthetic radioactive element; all its compounds are made and handled only in specialized nuclear laboratories.

elements.name: Plutonium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Plutonium is one of the strangest metals ever studied — it comes in seven different forms, changes size dramatically when heated, and is warm to the touch from its own radioactivity. It fuels nuclear weapons, but it also powers spacecraft that travel beyond the reach of sunlight.
funFacts: A lump of plutonium is warm to the touch because of its own radioactivity.
Plutonium exists in seven different crystal forms — more than any other element.
The Voyager probes, now beyond our solar system, still run on plutonium after 45 years.
The Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance are powered by plutonium.
It is named after Pluto, continuing the planet naming sequence after neptunium.

compounds.about: The fuel form used in reactors and space power sources.

compounds.name: Plutonium carbide
compounds.about: An experimental fast reactor fuel.

compounds.name: Plutonium nitrate
compounds.about: The soluble form used in fuel reprocessing.

compounds.name: Mixed oxide fuel
compounds.about: Plutonium and uranium oxides blended into reactor fuel.

compounds.name: Plutonium sesquioxide
compounds.about: A black oxide of the +3 state.

compounds.name: Plutonium hydride
compounds.about: Forms when plutonium metal meets hydrogen.

elements.compoundsNote: Plutonium is synthetic, radioactive and strictly controlled; all its chemistry happens inside secure nuclear facilities.

elements.name: Americium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Americium is the only synthetic element most people actually own — there is a speck of it inside many household smoke detectors, where its radiation senses smoke in the air. It was created during World War II and kept secret until after the war ended.
funFacts: There is a tiny amount of americium in many home smoke alarms.
It was discovered in 1944 but kept secret until 1945.
Its discovery was first announced to the public on a children's radio quiz show.
Americium is named after the Americas, matching europium in the row above.
The smoke alarm amount is so small and well shielded that it is completely safe.

compounds.name: Americium triiodide

compounds.name: Americium hydride
compounds.about: Formed when americium metal meets hydrogen.

elements.compoundsNote: Americium is entirely synthetic and radioactive; apart from the sealed source in smoke alarms, its compounds exist only in research laboratories.

elements.name: Curium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Curium honors Marie and Pierre Curie, the couple who pioneered the study of radioactivity. It glows purple in the dark and gives off so much heat that it can make itself red hot. Mars rovers carry curium to fire X-rays at rocks and work out what they are made of.
funFacts: Curium glows a beautiful purple-red in the dark.
It is so radioactive it heats itself and can glow red hot.
Mars rovers use curium to analyze the chemistry of Martian rocks.
It is named after Marie and Pierre Curie, who discovered radium and polonium.
Curium was actually discovered before americium, but announced afterwards.

compounds.name: Curium-244 source

elements.compoundsNote: Curium is synthetic and intensely radioactive, so its compounds are made only in specialized laboratories.

elements.name: Berkelium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Berkelium is named after the town of Berkeley in California, where the laboratory that discovered a whole string of new elements was based. Only a few grams have ever been made, and it played a starring role in creating element 117, tennessine.
funFacts: Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, home of the lab that found many new elements.
Less than a few grams have ever been produced in total.
Making 22 milligrams of it once took 250 days inside a reactor.
Berkelium was the target used to create tennessine, element 117.
It is one of the most expensive substances on Earth to produce.

elements.name: Californium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Californium is a neutron machine: a single microgram fires out 170 million neutrons every minute. That makes it genuinely useful — it starts up nuclear reactors, finds gold and oil underground, and scans luggage and cargo for hidden explosives.
funFacts: One microgram of californium releases about 170 million neutrons per minute.
It is one of the most expensive materials on Earth, worth millions per gram.
Californium neutron sources help find gold and oil deep underground.
Only about half a gram is made worldwide each year.
It is used to start up nuclear reactors, like a spark plug for an engine.

elements.name: Einsteinium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Einsteinium was found in a very surprising place: the fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952. Scientists flew planes through the cloud on filter paper and discovered two brand new elements. It is named after Albert Einstein, and it glows blue in the dark.
funFacts: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of a hydrogen bomb test.
It glows blue in the dark from its own intense radioactivity.
The discovery was kept secret for several years for military reasons.
Only a few milligrams have ever been made at once.
In 2021 scientists finally measured its basic chemistry for the first time.

elements.name: Fermium
elements.nameMeaning: After Enrico Fermi, the nuclear physicist

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Fermium was discovered alongside einsteinium in the fallout of the same hydrogen bomb test. It is the heaviest element that can be made in useful amounts inside a nuclear reactor — beyond fermium, scientists have to smash atoms together in particle accelerators instead.
funFacts: Fermium was found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test, in 1952.
It is named after Enrico Fermi, who built the first nuclear reactor.
Fermium is the last element that reactors can produce in weighable quantities.
Nobody has ever made enough fermium to see with the naked eye.
Its most stable form lasts about 100 days before decaying.

elements.name: Mendelevium

discovered.by: Ghiorso, Harvey, Choppin, Thompson and Seaborg

elements.nameMeaning: After Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who invented the periodic table itself. It was the first element ever discovered one atom at a time — the team made just seventeen atoms in their first experiment and had to identify them individually.
funFacts: The first experiment produced only seventeen atoms of mendelevium in total.
It is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table.
It was the first element identified by studying single atoms one by one.
Mendelevium is unusual among actinides for forming a fairly stable +2 state.
Every atom ever made has long since decayed away.
elements.compoundsNote: Mendelevium has never been produced in visible amounts — only a few million atoms have ever existed. No solid compounds have been isolated. Everything known about its chemistry comes from tracer experiments in solution, which show it forms Md³⁺ and, unusually, a stable Md²⁺ ion.

elements.name: Nobelium
elements.nameMeaning: After Alfred Nobel, founder of the Nobel Prizes

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite who founded the Nobel Prizes. Its discovery caused a long argument between Swedish, American and Soviet teams over who got there first — a dispute that took decades to settle.
funFacts: Three research teams claimed nobelium, causing a decades-long naming dispute.
It is named after Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite and founded the Nobel Prizes.
Nobelium is unusual because its +2 state is more stable than its +3 state.
That oddity comes from its completely full inner electron shell.
Only a few thousand atoms exist at any moment during an experiment.
elements.compoundsNote: Nobelium has never been isolated in weighable quantities and forms no known solid compounds. Its chemistry is known only from solution tracer studies, which revealed the surprising result that No²⁺ is its most stable ion — unlike every other actinide.

compoundsExamples.name: Nobelium(II) ion
compoundsExamples.about: Its most stable form, unusual among the actinides.

compoundsExamples.name: Nobelium(III) ion
compoundsExamples.about: Formed only with strong oxidizing agents.

elements.name: Lawrencium
elements.nameMeaning: After Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.description: Lawrencium is the last of the actinides, closing the bottom row of the periodic table. It is named after Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron — the atom-smashing machine that made discovering all these heavy elements possible in the first place.
funFacts: Lawrencium completes the actinide row of the periodic table.
It is named after the inventor of the cyclotron particle accelerator.
In 2015 scientists measured how tightly it holds its outermost electron — a rare feat.
Chemists still debate whether lawrencium belongs under lutetium in group 3.
Its longest-lived form survives only about 11 hours.
elements.compoundsNote: Lawrencium has never been produced in visible amounts and no compounds have been isolated. Solution experiments confirm it forms Lr³⁺, behaving much like the other heavy actinides.

compoundsExamples.name: Lawrencium(III) ion
compoundsExamples.about: Its only known form, confirmed by tracer chemistry.

elements.name: Rutherfordium
elements.nameMeaning: After Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬬻 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 卢, which supplies the sound “lú” and points to Rutherford 卢瑟福. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Rutherfordium is the first of the superheavy elements and the first beyond the actinide row. It is named after Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who discovered that atoms have a tiny dense nucleus at their center. It behaves chemically much like hafnium, just as the table predicts.
funFacts: Rutherfordium is the first element beyond the actinide series.
It is named after Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus.
Chemists proved it behaves like hafnium, confirming the periodic table still works this far out.
American and Soviet teams both claimed it, causing the 'Transfermium Wars'.
Its atoms survive for only about an hour at most.

compounds.name: Rutherfordium tetrachloride
compounds.about: Studied a few atoms at a time; behaves like hafnium chloride.

compounds.name: Rutherfordium tetrabromide
compounds.about: Detected in gas-phase chemistry experiments.

elements.compoundsNote: Only a handful of rutherfordium compounds have been observed, and never as visible material — chemists study them one atom at a time as they fly through a heated tube.

elements.name: Dubnium
elements.nameMeaning: After Dubna, the Russian town with a major nuclear laboratory

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬭊 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 杜, which supplies the sound “dù” and points to Dubna 杜布纳. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Dubnium is named after the Russian town of Dubna, home to one of the world's great nuclear research laboratories. The naming was part of a peace deal that finally ended years of arguing between American and Soviet scientists over who discovered which heavy element.
funFacts: Dubnium is named after a Russian town rather than a person.
Its name was chosen as part of a compromise ending the 'Transfermium Wars'.
It behaves chemically like tantalum and niobium, as the table predicts.
Its longest-lived atoms last only about a day.
Fewer than a few thousand atoms have ever been made.

compounds.name: Dubnium pentachloride
compounds.about: Observed in gas chemistry, behaving like niobium chloride.

compounds.name: Dubnium pentabromide
compounds.about: Detected in atom-at-a-time experiments.

compounds.name: Dubnium oxychloride
compounds.about: Formed when dubnium chloride meets oxygen.

elements.compoundsNote: Dubnium chemistry is done one atom at a time in gas streams; no compound has ever existed in a weighable amount.

elements.name: Seaborgium
elements.nameMeaning: After Glenn Seaborg, discoverer of ten elements

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬭳 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 喜, which supplies the sound “xǐ” and points to Seaborg 西博格. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Seaborgium is named after Glenn Seaborg, who helped discover ten different elements — more than anyone else in history. It was controversial at the time because Seaborg was still alive, and until then elements had only been named after people who had died.
funFacts: Glenn Seaborg was the first living person to have an element named after him.
He helped discover ten elements, more than any other scientist.
Seaborg could write his home address entirely in chemical element names.
Seaborgium behaves like tungsten and molybdenum, just as predicted.
Its atoms last only a couple of minutes.

compounds.name: Seaborgium oxychloride
compounds.about: Observed in gas chemistry, matching tungsten's behavior.

compounds.name: Seaborgium trioxide
compounds.about: Inferred from gas-phase oxide experiments.

compounds.name: Seaborgium oxyhydroxide
compounds.about: Detected in solution chemistry with just a few atoms.

elements.compoundsNote: Seaborgium compounds have only ever existed as single molecules, identified by tracking individual atoms as they decay.

elements.name: Bohrium

discovered.by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg and team

elements.nameMeaning: After Niels Bohr, who explained the structure of the atom

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬭛 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 波, which supplies the sound “bō” and points to Bohr 玻尔. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Bohrium honors Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist who worked out how electrons are arranged around the nucleus — the very idea that makes the periodic table make sense. Only a few atoms of bohrium have ever been made, each lasting a fraction of a minute.
funFacts: Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, who explained how electrons orbit the nucleus.
It was first made by firing chromium atoms at bismuth at enormous speed.
Chemists confirmed it behaves like rhenium, its lighter relative.
Its atoms exist for only about a minute at most.
The name was almost 'nielsbohrium' before the shorter version won.

compounds.name: Bohrium oxychloride
compounds.about: The one bohrium compound ever observed, in gas-phase chemistry.

elements.compoundsNote: Exactly one bohrium compound has been observed — and only as six individual molecules, detected one at a time in 2000.

elements.name: Hassium

discovered.by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg and team

elements.nameMeaning: From Hassia, Latin for the German state of Hesse

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬭶 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 黑, which supplies the sound “hēi” and points to Hesse 黑森. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Hassium is predicted to be the densest element of all, even heavier for its size than osmium. Chemists managed something remarkable with it: they made hassium tetroxide and showed it behaves just like osmium's version, proving the periodic table holds up even here.
funFacts: Hassium is calculated to be the densest element in the periodic table.
It is named after Hesse, the German state where it was discovered.
Chemists have made hassium tetroxide, one of the heaviest molecules studied.
Its atoms survive for only about ten seconds.
The experiment proving its chemistry used just a handful of atoms.

compounds.name: Hassium tetroxide
compounds.about: Successfully made and studied — it behaves just like osmium tetroxide.

compounds.name: Sodium hassate
compounds.about: Formed when hassium tetroxide meets sodium hydroxide.

elements.compoundsNote: Hassium tetroxide is one of the great achievements of superheavy chemistry — made and identified from only a few atoms.

elements.name: Meitnerium

discovered.by: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg and team

elements.nameMeaning: After Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 鿏 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 麦, which supplies the sound “mài” and points to Meitner 迈特纳. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner, the physicist who worked out how nuclear fission happens. She was overlooked for the Nobel Prize her collaborator received, so naming an element after her helped set the record straight. Only a few atoms have ever been created.
funFacts: Lise Meitner explained nuclear fission but was passed over for the Nobel Prize.
Meitnerium is one of only a few elements named after a woman.
Fewer than a hundred atoms of it have ever been made.
The very first experiment created just one single atom.
Its chemistry has never been studied — atoms decay too fast.
elements.compoundsNote: No meitnerium compounds are known. Too few atoms have ever been made, and they decay in a fraction of a second — far too quickly for any chemistry experiment.

elements.name: Darmstadtium

discovered.by: Hofmann, Ninov and team at GSI Darmstadt

elements.nameMeaning: After Darmstadt, the German city where it was made

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𫟼 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 达, which supplies the sound “dá” and points to Darmstadt 达姆施塔特. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Darmstadtium is named after the German city of Darmstadt, whose heavy-ion research laboratory discovered six different elements. Making it takes days of firing nickel atoms at lead at huge speed, and even then only a single atom might appear.
funFacts: The Darmstadt laboratory discovered six elements, from bohrium to copernicium.
Making darmstadtium can take a week of continuous atom-smashing for one atom.
It is predicted to behave a little like platinum.
Its atoms last only about ten seconds at the very most.
Only a few dozen atoms have ever existed.
elements.compoundsNote: No darmstadtium compounds are known. Its atoms decay far too quickly, and too few have been produced, for any chemistry to be attempted.

elements.name: Roentgenium

discovered.by: Hofmann and team at GSI Darmstadt

elements.nameMeaning: After Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𬬭 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 仑, which supplies the sound “lún” and points to Roentgen 伦琴. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Roentgenium honors Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics. It sits directly below gold on the periodic table, so scientists expect it would be a metal — though nobody has ever made enough to look at.
funFacts: It is named after the discoverer of X-rays, Wilhelm Röntgen.
Roentgenium sits below gold and silver in the periodic table.
Its name was announced on the 110th anniversary of the discovery of X-rays.
Only a few dozen atoms have ever been created.
Some calculations suggest it might not be shiny like gold at all.
elements.compoundsNote: No roentgenium compounds are known. Its atoms survive only seconds, and far too few have been made for any chemical study.

elements.name: Copernicium

discovered.by: Hofmann and team at GSI Darmstadt

elements.nameMeaning: After Nicolaus Copernicus, who put the Sun at the center

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 鿔 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 哥, which supplies the sound “gē” and points to Copernicus 哥白尼. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Copernicium is named after Nicolaus Copernicus, who realized the Earth goes around the Sun. Strangely, scientists think copernicium might be a gas or a liquid at room temperature, like mercury below which it sits — because it is so heavy that Einstein's relativity changes its chemistry.
funFacts: Copernicium may be a gas at room temperature, which would be extraordinary for a metal.
Its odd behavior comes from relativity: its electrons move near the speed of light.
It is named after Copernicus, who showed the Earth orbits the Sun.
It sits directly below mercury, the only liquid metal.
Experiments suggest it behaves more like a noble gas than a metal.
elements.compoundsNote: No copernicium compounds have been isolated. Gas-phase experiments show its atoms stick weakly to gold surfaces, hinting that it behaves more like a noble gas than like mercury.

compoundsExamples.name: Copernicium on gold
compoundsExamples.about: The only chemical interaction ever measured, from a few single atoms.

elements.name: Nihonium

discovered.by: Kosuke Morita's team at RIKEN, Japan

elements.nameMeaning: From Nihon, the Japanese name for Japan

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 鿭 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 尔, which supplies the sound “nǐ” and points to Nihon 日本. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Nihonium was the first element ever discovered in Asia, and it is named with the Japanese word for Japan. The team fired zinc at bismuth for nine years and produced just three atoms — an extraordinary display of patience.
funFacts: Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia.
The team searched for nine years and found only three atoms.
Nihon means 'land of the rising sun' — the Japanese name for Japan.
One atom appeared after 553 days of continuous experiment running.
It sits below thallium in the periodic table.
elements.compoundsNote: No nihonium compounds are known. Only a handful of atoms have ever existed, each lasting a fraction of a second.

elements.name: Flerovium
elements.nameMeaning: After Georgy Flerov, founder of the Dubna laboratory

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𫓧 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 夫, which supplies the sound “fū” and points to Flerov 弗廖罗夫. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Flerovium sits in the middle of what scientists call the 'island of stability' — a predicted region where superheavy atoms might last much longer than their neighbors. Its atoms do survive noticeably longer than expected, which is exciting evidence that the island is real.
funFacts: Flerovium may sit near the predicted 'island of stability' of long-lived superheavy atoms.
Its atoms last a few seconds, remarkably long for an element this heavy.
It is named after Georgy Flerov, who founded the Dubna laboratory.
Like copernicium, it may behave more like a gas than a metal.
It sits below lead in the periodic table.
elements.compoundsNote: No flerovium compounds are known. Gas-phase experiments on single atoms suggest it is surprisingly unreactive, possibly behaving more like a noble gas than like lead.

elements.name: Moscovium
elements.nameMeaning: After the Moscow region of Russia

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 镆 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 莫, which supplies the sound “mò” and points to Moscow 莫斯科. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Moscovium is named after the Moscow region, where the Dubna laboratory sits. It is one of the newest additions to the periodic table, officially named in 2016, and only a few dozen atoms have ever been created.
funFacts: Moscovium was officially added to the periodic table in 2016.
It is named after the Moscow region of Russia.
Only about a hundred atoms have ever been made.
Its atoms last less than a second before decaying.
It sits below bismuth in the periodic table.
elements.compoundsNote: No moscovium compounds are known. Its atoms decay in well under a second — far too fast for any chemistry experiment.

elements.name: Livermorium
elements.nameMeaning: After Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 𫟷 was invented for this element. It is built from 钅 — meaning it is a metal — plus 立, which supplies the sound “lì” and points to Livermore 利弗莫尔. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Livermorium is named after the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, whose scientists worked with the Russian team at Dubna to create several new elements. It sits below polonium, and only a few dozen atoms have ever existed.
funFacts: Livermorium came from a partnership between American and Russian laboratories.
It is named after the Lawrence Livermore laboratory in California.
Its atoms survive for only a few thousandths of a second.
It sits below polonium in the periodic table.
It was officially named in 2012.
elements.compoundsNote: No livermorium compounds are known. Its atoms exist for only milliseconds, making chemistry impossible with current techniques.

elements.name: Tennessine

discovered.by: Dubna, Oak Ridge and Livermore collaboration

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 鿬 was invented for this element. It is built from 石 — meaning it is a solid nonmetal — plus 田, which supplies the sound “tián” and points to Tennessee 田纳西. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Tennessine was the last gap in the seventh row of the periodic table to be filled. Making it required a rare target of berkelium, produced in Tennessee and flown to Russia — the berkelium was decaying the whole time, so the experiment had a strict deadline.
funFacts: Tennessine filled the very last empty space in row seven of the periodic table.
Its berkelium target had to be flown from Tennessee to Russia before it decayed.
It is named after the US state of Tennessee.
Only about twenty atoms have ever been made.
It sits below astatine, so it is technically a halogen — but may not act like one.
elements.compoundsNote: No tennessine compounds are known. Its atoms last only a few hundredths of a second, and fewer than two dozen have ever been made.

elements.name: Oganesson
elements.nameMeaning: After Yuri Oganessian, the superheavy element pioneer

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

elements.zhCharacterNote: 鿫 was invented for this element. It is built from 气 — meaning it is a gas — plus 奥, which supplies the sound “ào” and points to Oganessian 奥加涅相. One half tells you what it is, the other half tells you how to say it.
elements.description: Oganesson is the heaviest element known and closes the periodic table as we have it today. It sits in the noble gas column, but scientists think it would actually be a solid, not a gas, and might even be reactive — its huge, fast-moving electrons break the usual rules.
funFacts: Oganesson is the heaviest element ever created, closing the periodic table.
Only about five atoms have ever been made, each lasting under a millisecond.
Despite sitting with the noble gases, it is predicted to be a solid, not a gas.
Yuri Oganessian is only the second living person to have an element named after him.
Its electrons move so fast that Einstein's relativity reshapes its chemistry.
elements.compoundsNote: No oganesson compounds are known or ever likely to be made with current technology. Only a few atoms have ever existed, each for less than a thousandth of a second. Theory predicts it would be far more reactive than the other noble gases.
